parole.testo: From Old Swedish -aktogher, borrowed from Middle Low German -achtig, from -haftich (see German -haft). Cognate to Danish -agtig, Dutch -achtig, German -haft.

parole.significato: -able; create an adjective from a noun or verb
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -bar, borrowed from Middle Low German -bar, from Old Saxon -bari. Cognate with native Old Swedish -bǣr (Old Norse -bærr), German -bar (from Old High German -bāri), Dutch -baar, Old English -bære.

parole.significato: -ate, -ize; make a verb from a noun, similar to Swedish -a; used on loan-words with French -er and German -ieren
parole.testo: Attested already in Late Old Swedish. Derives from at least two distinct sources: # Borrowed from Middle Low German -êren, from Latin -ēre, ‑ĕre. # Borrowed from French -er, from Latin -āre (often via High German transmission). In this form, the suffix appears as an element of -isera.

parole.significato: -fold; suffixing a number, creating an adjective
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German -valdich, equivalent to -fald + -ig. Compare Danish -foldig, Dutch -voudig.

parole.significato: Productive suffix giving an adjective a nounal meaning; -ness, -ity
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -het, which is borrowed from Middle Low German -heit, from Proto-Germanic *haiduz. Cognate with Danish -hed, German -heit, Dutch -heid, English -hood.

parole.significato: -y; forms adjectives from nouns and verbs
parole.testo: From earlier -ig, -og, from Middle Low German -ich and Old Swedish -ogher, from Old Norse -agr, -ugr, -igr, from Proto-Germanic *-gaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos. Cognate with Old English -ig, whence English -y. Compare -og, avog, avig and -ot.
From Old Swedish -makare, a calque of Middle Low German -maker. Compare Danish -mager, Norwegian -maker.
From Middle Low German -makerije.

parole.significato: Signifies a female (particularly after professions and nationalities); -ess
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -ska, from Middle Low German -sche.

parole.significato: alas, oh (exclamation of sorrow, awe, etc. – being moved by emotion)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish akh, from Middle Low German ach (“an unhappy interjection”).

parole.significato: stern (the rear part or after end of a ship or vessel)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German achter, from Old Saxon aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after. Cognate with Swedish efter, Dutch achter, English after.

parole.significato: used as a verb particle, similar to German preposition an (“at, in, on, to”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German an and German an, and less commonly from English on, from Proto-Germanic *ana (“on, at”), cognate with English on and doublet of Swedish å, Swedish på.

parole.significato: to adopt (behavior, customs, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish anama, annama, anamma, annamma, from Middle Low German annamen (“receive”), from an (akin to on) + nemen (akin to German nehmen (“to take”), English nim and Swedish förnimma), influenced by the noun anname (“receiption, act of receiving”). Cognate with Danish annamme, Norwegian Bokm
From Old Swedish anfal, from Middle Low German anval.

parole.significato: important, urgent (of an issue or the like)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German angelegen, from Old Saxon ana- + liggian (“to be situated”).

parole.significato: to concern (have (legitimate) relevance to someone's interests)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German angan or German angehen. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål angå, Danish angå and Dutch aangaan. Equivalent to an- + gå.
Borrowed from Middle Low German anholden, equivalent to an- + hålla. Compare German anhalten, Danish anholde, Dutch aanhouden.

parole.significato: a malleolus (on either side of the ankle joint)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ankel, enkel.
Borrowed from Middle Low German ankōmen. Equivalent to an- + komma. Compare German ankommen, Dutch aankomen, English oncome.
Borrowed from Middle Low German anmoden. Cognate of German anmuten, Danish anmode.

parole.significato: to be of an opinion, to think, to believe, to feel
parole.testo: From Old Swedish anse, from Middle Low German ansen. Equivalent to an- + se.

parole.significato: a face; front side of the head
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ansichte. By surface analysis, an- + sikt (“sight”) + -e. Cognate with Danish ansigt, Norwegian ansikt. Compare also German Ansicht, Dutch aanzicht (“view”) and Angesicht, aangezicht (“face”).

parole.significato: a claim (laying claim to, for example ownership, authorship, a right, or a title)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ansprake (“address; polite and formal approach”), related to German Ansprache, equivalent to an- + språk. Compare Danish ansprog, Dutch aanspraak, German Anspruch.
From Middle Low German anstellen, equivalent to an- + ställa. Compare Dutch aanstellen.
From Middle Low German anstant.
From Middle Low German anstot. Compare Danish anstød, Norwegian Bokmål anstøt, Dutch aanstoot.

Apocopic form of antaga, calqued from Middle Low German annemen or German annehmen. All compounds with the verb ta have gone through apocope and those forms are now the standard ones, see also avta/avtaga, inta/intaga and överta/övertaga. Cognate with Danish antage, Norwegian Bokmål anta, Norwegian
Compound of an (“on”) + tasta (“to touch”), via pattern from Middle Low German antasten, albeit tasta (same as Middle Low German tasten) from Vulgar Latin *tastare, from *taxitare, from Latin taxare.
Borrowed from Middle Low German anwenden. Compare Norwegian Bokmål anvende.

parole.significato: to work, to be employed to do
parole.testo: From Old Swedish arbeida, arbeta, from Middle Low German arbeiden (“to work”), from Old Saxon arvēdian (“to offer”), from Proto-Germanic *arbaidijaną, from *arbaidiz (“labour, work, toil, hardship, suffering”), equivalent of arbete + -a. Compare Norwegian arbeide, Norwegian Nynorsk arbeide, arbeida,

parole.significato: work, job (economic role for which a person is paid)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish arbeide, from Middle Low German arbet, from Old Saxon arvēd. Compare Norwegian arbeid, Danish arbejde, Faroese arbeiði, German Arbeit, Dutch arbeid. Compare the doublet arvode, inherited from Old Swedish arvoþe, ærviþi, from Old Norse erfiði.

parole.significato: a sheet of paper (for writing on)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ark, from Middle Low German ark, from Latin arcus (“bow”). Compare German Bogen. It refers to the bend of the parchment when folded.

From Old Swedish armborst, from Middle Low German armborst, from Medieval Latin arcuballista, arbalista, from arcus + ballista. First attested in the early 14th century. Compare Danish and Norwegian armbrøst, German Armbrust, English arbalest.
From Old Swedish art, from Middle Low German art, from Old Saxon *ard, from Proto-Germanic *ardiz (“character, nature, inborn quality”).

parole.significato: Carrion, carcass (of an animal killed by a predator).
parole.testo: From Middle Low German âs. Cf. German Aas, Dutch aas.
From Middle Low German afbrek, from breken (“to break”). Equivalent to av + bräck. Compare Dutch afbrek, Danish afbræk.

parole.significato: retired, no longer on active duty
parole.testo: From Middle Low German afdanken. Compare German abdanken.
Inherited from Old Swedish afgrund, from Middle Low German afgrunt. Cognate of German Abgrund.

parole.significato: indulgence (release from the expectation of punishment in purgatory)
parole.testo: Old Swedish aflat, from Middle Low German aflat (“forgiveness”), from verb aflaten (“to forgive, to pardon”), equivalent to av- (“off”) + låta (“to allow, to let”). Cognate with Icelandic aflát, Danish aflad, German Ablass, Dutch aflaat.

parole.significato: a filled pastry or portion-sized cake
parole.testo: From Middle Low German backelse (“that which is baked”). Cognate with Low German Backelse.
From Old Swedish balia, from Middle Low German ballie, from French baille.

parole.significato: a trajectory, a course, a path (path that something moves along, especially in physics, astronomy, or the like)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bāne, from Old Saxon *bana, from Proto-West Germanic *banu, from Proto-Germanic *banō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-.
From Middle Low German bange, formed from be- + enge (from Old Saxon engi, angi (“narrow”)). Related to English angst and anger.

From Old Swedish barmhærtogher, barmhiærtogher, from Middle Low German barmhertich, apparently a calque of Latin misericors, from miser + cor. The first part is related to arm (“poor, weak”) and the second part in erbarmlig and the latter is related to hjärta (“heart”). Cognate with Danish barmhjert

Borrowed from Middle Low German barsch, from Old Saxon *barsk, from Proto-Germanic *barskaz, from *barsaz (“perch, bass”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰórs-o-s, from *bʰers- (“top, tip, point”). Related to borst, borste, -borre (in abborre, sjöborre and kardborre), (possibly) barr (as in granbarr), b
Inherited from Old Swedish bebodha, bebudha, from Middle Low German beboden. Equivalent to be- + båda. Cognate of Danish bebude.

From Old Swedish bedragha, from Middle Low German bedregen, from Old Saxon bidriogan, from Proto-West Germanic *bidreugan. By surface analysis, be- + draga, etymologically equivalent to be- + dryga. Displaced native svika in this sense.

parole.significato: to operate, to run, to manage
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bedriva, from Middle Low German bedrîven. Equivalent to be- + driva. Cognate with Danish bedrive, Norwegian Bokmål bedrive, German betreiben, Dutch bedrijven and English bedrive.
Derived from Middle Low German bedroven, from Proto-Germanic *drōbijaną. Cognate of Danish bedrøve, Dutch bedroeven, German betrüben.
Borrowed from Middle Low German bedüren. By surface analysis, be- + dyr (“dear”) + -a. Cognate of Danish bedyre, German beteuern.
After either Middle Low German bedoven, Low German bedöwen or German betäuben. By surface analysis, be- + döva (“dampen”). Cognate of Danish bedøva.
From Old Swedish befælla, from Middle Low German bevelen, from Old Saxon bifelhan. Displaced native bjuda in this sense. Compare Norwegian befale, German befehlen, Old English befēolan.
From Middle Low German bevaren or older German befahren, to be- + fara (“danger”) + -a.

parole.significato: to involve oneself (in), to get involved (with), to concern oneself (with), to deal (with) (usually of something or som…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish befata, from Middle Low German bevaten. By surface analysis, be- + fatta. Cognate of Danish befatte, German befassen, Dutch bevatten.

parole.significato: to be located (at); to be (positioned) at
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bevinden, from Old Saxon bifindan. Equivalent to be- + finna. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål befinne, Danish befinde, German befinden, Dutch bevinden (“to find”), English befind and Saterland Frisian befiende (“to be located”).

parole.significato: to liberate, to free, to make free
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bevrien and German befreien. Cognate with Danish befri, Norwegian Bokmål befri, Yiddish באַפֿרײַען (bafrayen), Middle Dutch bevrien, older Dutch bevrijen, now bevrijden, West Frisian befrije, Old English befrēoġan, Middle English *befreen, *bifreen and English befree. Equivale
Borrowed from Middle Low German bevrundet. Cognate with English befriended, Dutch bevriend, German befreundet.

parole.significato: to bury; to perform a burial
parole.testo: From Old Swedish begrava, from Middle Low German begrāven, from Proto-Germanic *bigrabaną. Equivalent to be- + gräva.
Borrowed from Middle Low German begripen, from Old Saxon bigrīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *bigrīpan. Equivalent to be- + gripa.

From Middle Low German beginnen, from Old Saxon biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną. Compare Danish begynde, Norwegian Bokmål begynne, Norwegian Nynorsk begynne, begynna, Low German begünnen, North Frisian begin, Saterland Frisian beginne, West Frisian begjinne, Scots begin, English begin, Dutc

parole.significato: to request, to ask for (ask for to be granted)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German begeren (“to want, covet”).

parole.significato: to commit, to perpetrate (perform, carry out)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bega, from Middle Low German begen. Equivalent to be- + gå.
Equivalent to be- + gåva, from Old Swedish begava, from Middle Low German begaven, from Old Saxon bi- + gevan. Compare Danish begave, Dutch begaven, German begaben.
From Old Swedish begava, from Middle Low German begaven.

parole.significato: to please (to make happy or satisfy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish behagha, from Middle Low German behagen, from Old Saxon bihagōn. Cognate with Danish behage, Norwegian Bokmål behage, German behagen and Dutch behagen.
From Old Swedish behagheligh, from Middle Low German behagelik, from the verb behagen, from Old Saxon bihagon (“to please, be suitable”).
Old Swedish behof, borrowed from Middle Low German behof, from Old Saxon *bihōf, from Proto-West Germanic *bihōf.

parole.significato: to keep; to maintain possession of
parole.testo: From Old Swedish behalda, beholda, from Middle Low German beholden, from Old Saxon bihaldan.

From Old Swedish beklagha, from Middle Low German beklagen. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål beklage, Norwegian Nynorsk beklage, beklaga, Danish beklage, German beklagen, Dutch beklagen. Equivalent to be- + klaga.
From Middle Low German bekomen, from Old Saxon biqueman, bikuman, from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną. Equivalent to be- + komma.

From Middle Low German bekreften or German bekräften (rare, more often bekräftigen), from Middle High German bekreften. Equivalent of be- + kraft + -a. The synonym bekräftiga went out of use during the 17th century. Cognate with Danish bekræfte, Norwegian Bokmål bekrefte and Norwegian Nynorsk bekref

parole.significato: trouble, difficulty; something which causes worry
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish bekymber, likely from Middle Low German bekummer. Superficially deverbal from bekymra.

parole.significato: to worry (oneself or someone with something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish bekymbra, from Middle Low German bekummeren, bekumberen. For the second element see German Kummer (“sorrow, grief”). Cognate of Dutch bekommeren, German bekümmern.
From Old Swedish bekænna, from Middle Low German bekennen. Equivalent of be- + känna. Cognate with Danish bekende, Norwegian Bokmål bekjenne, German bekennen and Dutch bekennen.
Likely borrowed from Middle Low German. Compare Dutch belakken.

parole.significato: to subject to a (physical or more abstract) load
parole.testo: From Middle Low German belasten. Equivalent to be- + lasta. Cognate with Danish belaste and Dutch belasten.
Borrowed from Middle Low German beleitsagen, equivalent to be- + ledsaga. Regarding shift in sense, compare German begleiten, French accompagner.
From Old Swedish belæghin, from Middle Low German belegen, the past participle of Middle Low German beliggen.

parole.significato: to impose, to subject (to a punishment, fine, tariff, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish belæggia, from Middle Low German beleggen, equivalent to be- + lägga. Compare Danish belægge, Dutch beleggen, English belay, German belegen.

From Old Swedish belæghra, from Middle Low German belegeren. By surface analysis, be- + lägra. Cognate of Danish belejre, Dutch belegeren, German belagern, English beleaguer. Doublet of ligga and lägga. Compare with origin for läger.

From Middle Low German belonen or German belohnen, equivalent to be- + löna. Cognate with Danish belønne, Norwegian Bokmål belønne, Dutch belonen, Afrikaans beloon, Limburgish beloene, West Frisian beleanje, Saterland Frisian beloonje, Luxembourgish belounen and Yiddish באַלוינען (baloynen).

parole.significato: to man (to take up position in order to operate something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bemanna, from Middle Low German bemannen, equivalent to be- + man (“a man”) + -a. Cognate with Danish bemande, Norwegian Bokmål bemanne, Norwegian Nynorsk bemanna, bemanne, German bemannen, Dutch bemannen and English beman.

From Old Swedish benæghin, likely from unattested Middle Low German *genegen (equivalent to Dutch genegen), past participle of Middle Low German nigen (“to bend; to bow down”). Compare German geneigt. Doublet of niga.

Probably from Middle Low German berēkenen, equivalent to be- + räkna. Cognate with Danish beregne, Norwegian Bokmål beregne, Norwegian Nynorsk berekne, berekna, Dutch berekenen, Low German beräknen, German berechnen, West Frisian berekkenje.

parole.significato: to tell (convey – a story, account, information, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish berætta, from Middle Low German berichten, in correspondence to Swedish rätta (verb) and rätt (verb and noun), equivalent to be- + rätt + -a or be- + rätta. Cognate with Danish berette, Norwegian Bokmål berette, Dutch berichten (“to report”), berechten (“to judge, to try”), bericht
Calque of Middle Low German berom, equivalent to a deverbal from berömma.
From Old Swedish berøma, from Middle Low German berômen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- + *hrōmiz (“fame, glory”). Compare German berühmen. Related to rosa (“to praise, to commend”).

From Old Swedish beroren, from Middle Low German beroren, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”), *hrōzijaną (“to stir”), equivalent to be- + röra. Cognate with Danish berøre, Norwegian Bokmål berøre, German berühren and Dutch beroeren.

Inherited from Old Swedish berøva, from Middle Low German beroven, from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną. By surface analysis, be- + röva. Cognate of Danish berøve, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌱𐍉𐌽 (biraubōn), Dutch beroven, English bereave.

parole.significato: seal (affix a seal in order to prove authenticity or attest to accuracy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish besighla, from Middle Low German besigelen, from Old Saxon *bisiglian, from Proto-West Germanic *bisigilōn. Cognate of Danish besegle, Dutch bezegelen, German besiegeln. Related to försegla, insegel, sigill.
From Old Swedish besinna, from Middle Low German besinnen. Equivalent to be- + sinne + -a. Compare Danish besinde, Dutch bezinnen.

From Old Swedish besitia, from Middle Low German besitten, from Proto-Germanic *bisitjaną, from *bi- + *sitjaną. Equivalent to be- + sitta. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål besitte, Danish besidde, Dutch bezitten, German besitzen, English besit and Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (bisitan).

parole.significato: answer, information; that to inform or let somebody know
parole.testo: From Old Swedish beskedh, from Middle Low German besched (“wit”), from bescheden (“to separate, to explain”).
From Middle Low German bescheten or German beschießen, equivalent to be- + skjuta. Compare Danish beskyde, Dutch beschieten.

From Old Swedish beskriva, from Middle Low German beschrîven, bescrîven, equivalent to be- + skriva (“to write”). Cognate with Danish beskriva, Norwegian Bokmål beskrive, Norwegian Nynorsk beskriva, beskrive, Dutch beschrijven, Afrikaans beskryf, Limburgish besjrieve, German beschreiben, Yiddish באַ
Inherited from Old Swedish beskydda, borrowed from Middle Low German beschudden. Compare Danish beskytte, Dutch beschutten, German beschützen.
Equivalent to be- + skylla. Likely borrowed from unattested Middle Low German *beschulden. Cognate of Danish beskylde. Compare Dutch beschuldigen, German beschuldigen.
From Middle Low German bescheftig. Compare German geschäftig.
From Old Swedish beslut, from Middle Low German beslut, a deverbal from besluten. First attested in 1513. Compare Dutch besluit, German Beschluss.

parole.significato: to decide, to make a decision
parole.testo: From Old Swedish besluta, from Middle Low German besluten. First attested in 1504. Cognate with Danish beslutte. Compare Dutch besluiten, German beschließen.

parole.significato: to feed, to give food, usually on a greater scale, e.g. in a school or in the military
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bespisa, from Middle Low German bespisen. Compare German bespeisen.
From Old Swedish bestenduger, a borrowing of Middle Low German bestendich. Attested since 1645.

parole.significato: a population (of similar things, usually animals or plants – sometimes more generally), a set
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bestand, bestandt, bestondh, from Middle Low German bestant.

parole.significato: to beg, to ask (someone), to adjure
parole.testo: From Old Swedish besværia, from Middle Low German besweren. Equivalent to be- + svärja. Cognate with Danish besværge, Norwegian Bokmål besverge, Dutch bezweren and German beschwören.
From Middle Low German besetten, from Old Saxon *bisettian, from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan, from Proto-Germanic *bisatjaną (“to beset”), equivalent to be- + sätta.

parole.significato: to visit (to go and meet or see)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish besøkia, from Middle Low German besoken, equivalent to be- + söka. Cognate with Danish besøge, Norwegian Bokmål besøke, Norwegian Nynorsk besøke, besøka, besøkje, besøkja, Dutch bezoeken, German besuchen, Saterland Frisian besäike, English beseech, beseek and Scots beseik.
From Middle Low German bedanken, equivalent to be- + tacka. Compare Danish betakke, German bedanken, Dutch bedanken.

parole.significato: to pay; to give money in exchange for goods or services
parole.testo: From Old Swedish betala, bitala, bittala, from Middle Low German betalen, equivalent to be- + tala. Cognate with Danish betale, Norwegian Bokmål betale, Norwegian Nynorsk betala, betale, Dutch betalen, West Frisian betelje, German bezahlen, Low German betahlen and English betall. Displaced native gä
From Middle Low German beting or Dutch beting.

parole.significato: to regard (look at something (for a bit of time))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German betrachten. Equivalent to be- + trakta. Attested since the 14th century.

parole.significato: to set foot on, to tread on, to betread
parole.testo: From Middle Low German betreden and German betreten. Equivalent to be- + träda. Cognate with Danish betræde, Norwegian Bokmål betre, betrede, Dutch betreden and English betread.
Borrowed from Middle Low German bedwingen, equivalent to be- + tvinga. Cognate of Danish betvinge, Dutch bedwingen, German bezwingen.

From Old Swedish bethydha, from Middle Low German beduden, equivalent to be- + tyda. Cognate with Danish betyde, Norwegian Bokmål bety, Norwegian Nynorsk bety, German bedeuten, Vilamovian bydȧjta, Luxembourgish bedeiten, Dutch beduiden, older bedieden, Limburgish beduuje, Saterland Frisian betjuude

parole.significato: to attest, to testify, to bear witness to
parole.testo: From Old Swedish betygha, from Middle Low German betugen. Compare Dutch betuigen, German bezeugen.
From Old Swedish bethækkia, from Middle Low German bedecken, from Old Saxon *bithekkian, from Proto-West Germanic *biþakkjan, equivalent to be- + täcka.
From be- + and tänka, from Old Swedish þænkia, from Middle Low German denken (“to perceive, think”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German bedenklich. Cognate of Danish betænkelig, German bedenklich, Dutch bedenkelijk.

From Old Swedish bevara, from Middle Low German bewaren, from Proto-Germanic *biwarōną from *bi- + *warōną. Equivalent to be- + vara (“to last”). Cognate with English beware, Danish bevare, Norwegian Bokmål bevare, Norwegian Nynorsk bevare, bevara, Dutch bewaren and German bewahren. Displaced native
From Old Swedish bevekia, from Middle Low German beweken. Compare German bewegen, Dutch bewegen, Danish bevæge, English beweigh.

parole.significato: a proof (any effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bevis, likely borrowed from Middle Low German bewis. However, the Swedish term is attested from 1501, whereas the earliest known attestation of the Low German term is from 1575. Compare Danish bevis, Dutch bewijs, German Beweis.
Old Swedish bevænt, from Middle Low German bewent, past participle of Middle Low German bewenden (“relate; depend”).

parole.significato: to second, to agree as a second person; to support a suggestion
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bivallen. Compare Danish bifalde, Dutch bijvallen, German beifallen.

parole.significato: cheap; of low price, of little worth
parole.testo: From Middle Low German billik, billich, from Proto-West Germanic *bilalīk. Compare German billig and Dutch billijk.

From Old Swedish bisitiare, from Middle Low German bisitter (“bysitter”), equivalent to bi- + sitta + -are. Cognate of Danish bisidder, Dutch bijzitter, German Beisitzer, English bysitter. Compare Swedish assessor.
From Middle Low German blank, from Old Saxon blank, from Proto-West Germanic *blank. Displaced native Swedish black, from Old Norse blakkr.

Apocopic form of bliva, from Old Swedish bliva, from Middle Low German blîven (“to remain”), from Old Saxon bilīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *bilīban, from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną. Displaced Swedish varda completely in the present tense, and partly in the past tense.
From Old Swedish blidha, borrowed (likely through Middle Low German blîde) from Medieval Latin blida. Ultimately from Ancient Greek βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

parole.significato: a block, a boulder, a cuboid (of ice, wood, rock)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German block, from Old Saxon blok, from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką.
From Middle Low German blôt, from Old Saxon *blōt. Doublet of blöt. Compare German bloß, Dutch bloot, Danish blot.
From Old Swedish bokka, bukka, from Middle Low German bucken, from Old Saxon *bukkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bukkōn.
From Middle Low German boie or Middle Dutch boeye, from Old French buie (“fetter, chain”), itself of Germanic origin, from Frankish *baukn (“symbol, sign”).
From Old Swedish boia, from Middle Low German boie, from Old French buie, boie, from Latin boia (“neck-collar”).
Derived from Middle Low German bōlen, from bōle (“friend; lover; mistress”). Cognate of German buhlen and Dutch boelen. Compare origin of German Buhle.
Derived from Middle Low German *bomolie, literally "tree oil". Cognate of Dutch boomolie, German Baumöl. First attested in 1541.

parole.significato: to wax or polish a floor
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bônen, from Old Saxon *bōnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bōnōn. Cognate with Dutch boenen, German bohnern.
Borrowed from Middle Low German borchvrede or German Burgfrieden, equivalent to borg + fred.

From Old Swedish borghmæstare, borghamæstare, borgharamæstare, from Middle Low German borgemester, borgermester, equivalent to borg + mästare. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål borgermester, Norwegian Nynorsk borgarmeister, Danish borgmester (whence also Greenlandic borgmesteri), German Bürgermeister, D

parole.significato: a criminal, chiefly a thief or robber
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bōve, from Middle Low German bōve, from Proto-Germanic *bō-.
Derived from Middle Low German bokwete, equivalent to bok (“beech”) + vete (“wheat”). Related to Danish boghvede and possibly borrowed or calqued from it.
Borrowed from Middle Low German brikke. Cognate of French brique.
Borrowed from Middle Low German brill, brille (cognate of German Brille), from Latin bēryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos). Doublet of beryll and briljant.

parole.significato: to bring; to transport toward someone else
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German bringen, brengen, from Old Saxon brengian, bringan. Compare Dutch brengen, German bringen, English bring, West Frisian bringe.

parole.significato: brake; a device used to slow or stop a vehicle, by friction; often installed on the wheels, then often in the plural.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German premese. Compare German Bremse and Norwegian Nynorsk brems.
Borrowed from Middle Low German bromese, compare German Bremse and Sanskrit भ्रमर (bhramara). Replaced earlier Old Swedish brims, compare Norwegian Nynorsk brems.

parole.significato: to use to (present tense of used to); to be in the habit of
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bruken, from Old Saxon brukan.

parole.significato: to make a deep, humming or growling sound (of for example a bear, an engine, or a fan)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German brummen, from Old Saxon *brummōn, from Proto-West Germanic *brummōn.

parole.significato: strong desire to mate in animals, especially mammals; heat, rut
parole.testo: From Middle Low German brunst

parole.significato: to make noise like bad speakers, crashing waves, rapids, effervescent tablets dissolving, etc. – a sound like static; t…
parole.testo: Used in the Swedish Bible of 1541, same as Danish bruse (“roar, fizz”), from Middle Low German brûsen, compare German brausen.

parole.significato: to concern, to bother (one's head or the like with something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German brüden (“to torment, annoy; to ravish (a woman)”), with the same semantic development as the related Dutch bruien; attested since 1722.
From Middle Low German bruderie, from the same root as bry.
From Middle Low German breken, from Old Saxon brekan (“to break”).
From Old Swedish brækeliker, from Middle Low German brekelik, from breken (“to break”). Equivalent to bräcka + -lig. Cognate of Danish brækkelig. Compare German brechlich, gebrechlich.

parole.significato: any of a group of clear, strong liquors, including aquavit and vodka but also various unflavored beverages
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brännevin, brænnevin, calqued from Middle Low German bernewin. By surface analysis, bränna (“burn, as in distill”) + vin (“wine”). Akin to Norwegian brennevin, Icelandic brennivín and German Branntwein.
Borrowed from Middle Low German brok, equivalent to German Bruch, from Proto-Germanic *brukiz. Cognate of English breach.

parole.significato: to argue, to fight, to brawl, to make trouble
parole.testo: From Middle Low German brake, probably from or related to Proto-West Germanic *brekan. Compare Middle Dutch braak.

parole.significato: a dent (especially in sheet metal, e.g. on a car)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German bokele, from Old French bocle, from Latin buccula. Cognate with English buckle. "Trophy" sense possibly influenced by pokal.

parole.significato: a bulge, a bump (small, round, hard, tender swelling, especially one caused by a strike or blow)
parole.testo: Likely from Middle Low German būle, from Proto-Germanic *būlō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, inflate, swell up”). Doublet of ballong, boll, bolster, bulle, bälg, and bölja, and probably böld. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk bule and bole, Dutch buil, German Beule, English boil.

parole.significato: a bundle, a bunch (often of broad and flat or long and narrow objects, for example a stack of paper)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bunt, from Old Saxon *bund, from Proto-Germanic *bundą.
Borrowed from Middle Low German pardues, perduuz, pardus, perdus, likely onomatopoeic. Cognate with German bardaus, pardauz, Dutch pardoes, perdoes, Norwegian Bokmål bardus, and Danish bardus.

parole.significato: burghership, the right to pursue certain professions
parole.testo: bur (“burgher”) + -skap (“-ship”). From Old Swedish burskap, from Middle Low German būrschap. The word bur was used in the meaning "burgher" or "city inhabitant", but could also mean "villager", "farmer", or "neighbor". Compare Dutch buurschap, Dutch buurtschap, English burghership, German Bauerscha

Borrowed from Middle Low German bursprake. By surface analysis, bur (“burgher”) + språk. Originally in the sense of a townhall meeting. Current sense due to the bay window at Rådstugan, Stockholm, from whence proclamations of such meetings were made public. Compare origin of burbrev and burskap.
Borrowed from Middle Low German burs, buss (“comrade; boy”), further from Medieval Latin bursa (“purse”). Attested since 1697.
Borrowed from Middle Low German busse or Dutch bus (“cylindrical box”); related to bössa. Attested since 1804.

From Middle Low German büken, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *bōkijā (“beech”). Related to German bauchen and German bäuchen. Cognate of French buer and English buck (“to soak, steep or boil in lye or suds”).
From Old Swedish byksa (pl. byksor, "pair of pants") and Middle Low German buxe, cognate with Icelandic buxur, Danish buks, Norwegian bukse, Kashubian bùksë.
From Middle Low German bernsten, based on bernen (to burn), i.e. "a fiery stone", cognate with German Bernstein. Displaced native Swedish rav.

From Old Swedish bæver, from Middle Low German biber, bever, from Old Saxon biƀar, biƀor, from Proto-West Germanic *bebru, from Proto-Germanic *bebruz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰébʰrus. Displaced native bjur.
Borrowed from Middle Low German bāke, from Old Frisian bāken. Cognate of Old Saxon bōkan, English beacon.

From Old Swedish bolverk or bulværk, from Middle Low German bolwerk. Superficially equivalent to bål (“bole; stem; sturdy plank”) + verk. Doublet of bulevard. Cognate of German Bollwerk, Danish bolværk, Dutch bolwerk, English bulwark, French boulevard.
bång + styra + -ig, from Middle Low German balstūrich. Compare Danish balstyrig. First part of original compound cognate with Old Norse bǫl. Attested since 1605.
From Middle Low German bodel, from Old Saxon budil, from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz (“bailiff, one who carries out an order”).

parole.significato: gun (shooting weapon functioning through stored energy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish byssa, bössa (“rifle, cannon, box”), from Middle Low German büsse (“box, gun”), from Medieval Latin buxis, from Ancient Greek πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s), from πῠ́ξος (pŭ́xos, “box wood”). Doublet of bussa (“to fit with a bushing”). Cognate with bush.
The perfect participle of Middle Low German don, in other words: "done".
From Old Swedish del, from Middle Low German dēl, deil, from Old Saxon dēl.

Inherited from Old Swedish delaktogher, from Middle Low German delhaftich, delachtich, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *daili (“part, share”) + *haft (“captive”). Cognate of Danish delagtig, archaic Dutch deelachtich, German teilhaftig.
From Old Swedish doch, dogh, dog, thoch, thok, tog, from Middle Low German doch, from Old Saxon thōh‚ from Proto-West Germanic *þauh. Replaced native Old Swedish þo, from Old Norse þó.
From Middle Low German dolk, from Old Saxon *dalk, from Proto-West Germanic *dalk, from Proto-Germanic *dalkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰalg-, *dʰalk-.
From Middle Low German dōpe, from Old Saxon dōpi, from Proto-West Germanic *daupīni, from Proto-Germanic *daupīniz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-. Doublet of doppa and djup.

From Middle Low German düppen, from Old Saxon dopian, from Proto-West Germanic *daupijan, from Proto-Germanic *daupijaną, to dip (in a liquid), to immerse. See there for further descendants. Doublet of dop, döpa, and djup.

Inherited from Late Old Swedish dravant, dravantare, from Middle Low German dravant. Cognate of German Trabant. Further origin disputed. Suggested cognates include Italian trabante, Czech drobit, Persian دربان (darbân).

parole.significato: to strike, to affect, to hit, to befall (someone – affect someone, of something negative)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish drabba‚ from Middle Low German drapen. Doublet of dräpa and träffa. Compare English drub.
From draga + -are. In (sense 1.2), from Middle Low German dragen (“carry”) (compare German tragen).

parole.significato: to throw (form clay into objects with the help of a potter's wheel)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German dreien, from Old Saxon thrāian, from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną.
From Old Swedish drinkare, from Middle Low German drinker, equivalent to dricka + -are. Compare English drinker.
Borrowed from Middle Low German drîstich, from drîste + -ich, from Old Saxon thrīsti, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīstī. By surface analysis, drista + -ig.
From Middle Low German druppen, from or related to Old Saxon dropo (“a drop”).

parole.significato: someone ill-mannered or (socially) clumsy; an oaf
parole.testo: Disputed. Held by some to be borrowed from Middle Low German drummel (“lump”), more likely deverbal from drumla. Compare English drumble.
From Middle Low German drūve (“bunch”), from Old Saxon thrūvo, from Proto-West Germanic *þrūbō (compare German Traube (“bunch, grape”)), from Old High German drūbo).
From Old Swedish drāpliker, from Middle Low German draplik (“that hits the target”). Equivalent to dråp (“hit, strike”) + -lig (“-ly”).

parole.significato: good; talented; capable (showing good ability, in a sense that includes both being good at something and being well-beh…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German duchtich, from Old Saxon *duhtig, from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg (“strong, proficient”). Parallel borrowing with Danish dygtig, Norwegian dyktig.

parole.significato: a deep, loud noise like from a lightning bolt; booming, thunder
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German dunner, donder. Cognate of German Donner, English thunder, Dutch donder. Compare tordön.

parole.significato: a (usually plastic) container shaped somewhat like a jerry can
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tunneke, a diminutive of tunne (“barrel”), from Proto-Germanic *tunnǭ, *tunnō (“tun, barrel, cask”), from Latin tunna.
From Middle Low German dunst, from Old Saxon *dunst, from Proto-Germanic *dunstą. Cognate of German Dunst.
Inherited from Old Swedish dust, duster, diost, from Middle Low German dust, diost, from Old French joste, juste, from Latin juxta. Cognate of Danish dyst, French joute.
From Middle Low German dūken *ducken, from Old Saxon *dūkan *dukkan, from Proto-West Germanic *dūkan.
Equivalent to dyr + -bar, from Old Swedish dyrbar, from Middle Low German dūrbar. Cognate of Middle High German tiurbaer, German teuerbar, Dutch dierbaar, Danish dyrebar.

parole.significato: a lock pick, a tool for lock picking (instead of a key)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German diderik. Cognate of German Dietrich (“lockpick”), Danish dirk, Finnish tiirikka.

parole.significato: gloomy (feeling, expressing, or marked by gloom)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German dūster, from Old Saxon thiustri (“obscure, dark”).
From Old Swedish dämpa, from Middle Low German dempen, from Proto-Germanic *dampijaną.

parole.significato: drowsy (in a relaxed manner, for example after lying out in the sun)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German dosich, from Proto-West Germanic *dusīg. Cognate of English dizzy. By surface analysis, dåsa + -ig (“-y”).
From Middle Low German eigendōm, equivalent to egen + -dom. Compare German Eigentum, Danish ejendom, Dutch eigendom.
From Old Swedish ælænde, answering to Danish elende; from Middle Low German elende, ellende, from Proto-West Germanic *alljas (“other”) + *land (“land”).
Inherited from Old Swedish endräkt, from Middle Low German endrecht, eindrecht, endracht. Cognate of Danish endragt, Dutch eendracht, German Eintracht.

From Old Swedish enkil, from Middle Low German enkel, from Proto-Germanic *ainkila-, equivalent to en (“one”) + -el. Compare etymology of English simple. Cognate with Danish enkel, enkelt, Norwegian enkel, Icelandic ekkil, Dutch enkel and Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌺𐌻𐍃 (ainakls). Compare also Latin singulus with th
Inherited from Old Swedish ævigher, borrowed from Middle Low German êwich; related to Old Norse ævi.
From Middle Low German in der vôge fallen. Compare Danish falde til føje.
From Old Swedish falsker, borrowed from Middle Low German valsch, from Old Saxon *falski, from Proto-West Germanic *falskī (“false, counterfeit”).
Inherited from Old Swedish falsklika, falskeliga, from Middle Low German valschliken. Cognate of Dutch valschelijk, German fälschlich.
From Middle Low German vāre, vār, from Old Saxon *fāra, fār, from Proto-Germanic *fērō (“danger”), whence Old English fær, Old Norse fár, German Gefahr.
From Old Swedish fārliker, from Middle Low German varlik. Equivalent to fara + -lig.
From Middle Low German vart, from Old Saxon fard. Cognate with Dutch vaart, German Fahrt. Doublet of färd.

parole.significato: to grasp, take (hold in one's hand); the concrete meaning of grasp
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German vāten, from Old Saxon *fatōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fatōn, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną. Cognate with Danish fatte, Norwegian Bokmål fatte, Dutch vatten and German fassen.

Inherited from Old Swedish feghþ, feyd, borrowed from Middle Low German veide, from Old Saxon *fēhitha, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“enmity, feud”). Cognate of Old High German fēhida, German Fehde, Old English fǣhð.

From Middle Low German feil, from French faille (“fault, flaw”). See Norwegian feil and Danish fejl. Used in Swedish at least since 1527. For the adverb, the now obsolete form felt was the dominant written form until the mid 19th century.

parole.significato: a pocket (bag stitched to an item of clothing)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vicke, which could be borrowed from Italian ficcare (“to stick something in”). More at English fob. Cognate of Norwegian Nynorsk fikke (“waistcoat pocket”).

Derived from Middle Low German vīentlik, from vient + -lik, equivalent to fiende + -lig. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål fiendtlig, Norwegian Nynorsk fiendtleg, fiendsleg, Danish fjendtlig, German feindlich, Dutch vijandelijk and English fiendly.
From Middle Low German vīle, from Old Saxon fila, from Proto-West Germanic *fį̄hlu, from Proto-Germanic *finhlō. Cognate with English file and German Feile.
From Late Old Swedish filter, likely from Middle Low German vilt (same as Danish filt).
From Middle Low German vinke, from Old Saxon *fink, from Proto-Germanic *finkiz.

parole.significato: to celebrate (a person, happy occurrence, holiday, etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vîren, from Old Saxon fīrion, from Latin feriari. Compare German feiern, whence Danish fejre.

parole.significato: to lower (by letting out on a rope)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vîren, from Old French virer, of uncertain origin, but probably from Latin vībrare. If so, a doublet of vibrera. Compare Danish fire, English veer.
From Middle Low German vlabbe, flabbe (“gaping mouth”), from the Germanic prefix *flabb-, probably ultimately imitative. See English flap. Cognate with Danish flabbet.

parole.significato: a thin sharp piece of wood or rock or some other material that splinters easily; a splinter, a chip (of rock)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vlise, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *flint. Cognate with German Fliese, Old Norse flís.

From Old Swedish flit, from Middle Low German vlīt, vlît, from Old Saxon *flīt, from Proto-West Germanic *flīt, from Proto-Germanic *flītaz, for which compare *flītan (“to strive”). See also German Low German Fliet, Saterland Frisian Fliet, Dutch vlijt, Danish flid, Norwegian Bokmål flid, Norwegian
Inherited from Old Swedish fliteliker, from Middle Low German vlītich. By surface analysis, flit + -ig. Cognate of Danish flittig. Compare Dutch vlijtig, German fleißig.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vleder, further origin disputed. See German Flieder, Dutch vlier.
From Middle Low German vlögel (“wing”), equivalent to flyga (“to fly”) + -el (“agent suffix”). Doublet of flygel.
Borrowed from Middle Low German flöite, from Old French fleute.

From Old Swedish föghia, fögha; from Middle Low German vôgen, from Old Saxon fōgian, from Proto-Germanic *fōgijaną. Cognate with Dutch voegen, Old High German fuogen (“to add”) (German fügen), Old English fēġan (English fay). Doublet of fager, föga, få, and fånga.

parole.significato: an officer of the court, a bailiff
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fohgdhe, foghate, etc., from Middle Low German voget, from Latin vocatus, from advocatus. Doublet of advokat (“lawyer”).

Attested since 1609 according to Nationalencyklopedins Ordbok, from Middle Low German fôrt (“away, further, forward”), which is used adverbially (forts) with the same meaning in Low German, from Middle Low German fort, from Old Saxon forth. Related to för (“fore”), före (“before”) and forsla (“trans
Inherited from Old Swedish frakta, from Middle Low German vrachten. By surface analysis, frakt + -a. Cognate of English fraught.

parole.significato: French (of or pertaining to France or the French language)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German fransch, which goes back, via Old French franceis (French français), to Late Latin Franciscus. This adjective is borrowed from Frankish *frankisk (“Frankish”), which is also the source of English French (Old English Frenċisċ).
From Old Swedish franzoos, from Middle Low German frantzoser, from Old French françois. Cognate of German Franzose.
From Middle Low German vreidich.
From Middle Low German vri, from Old Saxon frī, from Proto-West Germanic *frī, from Proto-Germanic *frijaz.
From Middle Low German vrīmōdich, equivalent to fri + mod (“state of mind”) + -ig. Compare German freimütig.

From Old Swedish frisker, from Middle Low German vrisch, from Old Saxon *frisk, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-. Doublet of fresk, fräsch, and färsk.

parole.significato: religious in a quiet and serious way, pious
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fromber, from Middle Low German vrome, from Old Saxon fruma, from Proto-Germanic *frumô, related to Dutch vroom (“pious”).

parole.significato: to glut, to gorge, to feast (eat gluttonously)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vratzen. Cognate of German fressen, Norwegian fråtse and Danish fråse. Doublet of fräta. Attested as a verb since 1526, and as a noun since 1990.
From Old Swedish frokoster, from Middle Low German vrokost. For the components, compare German früh (“early”) and Old Norse kostr (“choice; food”).

parole.significato: to fear, to dread, to be afraid
parole.testo: From Old Swedish frukta, frokta, frykta, from Middle Low German vruchten, from Old Saxon forhtian, from Proto-West Germanic *furhtijan.

From Middle Low German vrouwentimmer from vrouwe + -n- + timmer. Cognate with Danish fruentimmer, Norwegian Bokmål fruentimmer, Norwegian Nynorsk fruentimmer, German Frauenzimmer and Dutch vrouwenzimmer.

parole.significato: corrode, to chemically damage or destroy a material with which the substance has come into contact
parole.testo: From Old Swedish frǣta, from Middle Low German vreten (“to eat savagely, stuff”), from Old Saxon fretan.
From Middle Low German vrāge (German Frage), from Proto-West Germanic *frāgu, from Proto-Germanic *frēgō. Compare English frain. Displaced native spörja (“to ask”), spörsmål (“question”).

parole.significato: Miss ((title for an) unmarried woman (of any class – see usage notes below))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish fröken, from Middle Low German vröuken, vrouwicken, diminutive of vrûwe, vrouwe (“woman, lady”), from Old Saxon frūa, from Proto-West Germanic *frauwjā.
From Middle Low German vuchtich (“moist”), derived from vucht (“moist, moisture”), from Old Saxon *fūht, from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht.

Old Swedish fulbordha, from Middle Low German vulborden, based on the noun vulbort (“full board, a ship built to completion”), from Old Saxon ful + bord which is from Proto-West Germanic *bord. The Old Swedish fulbordha was both a verb and adjective, still used as an adjective in the 1526 Bible tran
From Old Swedish fulænda, from Middle Low German vulenden, German vollenden. Superficially equivalent to full + ända, as in "to fully end". Attested since late 15th century.
Borrowed from Middle Low German fürbake. By surface analysis, fyr + båk.
From Old Swedish fækta, from Middle Low German vechten, from Old Saxon fehtan, from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan, from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną. Compare Dutch vechten and English fight.

parole.significato: a field, a (physical) area, an open space in a landscape (for farming or battle)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fält, from Middle Low German velt, from Old Saxon feld, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu, cognate with Old English feld, English field, also related to fjäll.

parole.significato: colour; the spectral composition of visible light
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish færgha, from Middle Low German verwe or varwe, from Proto-Germanic *farwō. Cognate with German Farbe, Danish farve, Dutch verf and Norwegian farge.
From Old Swedish färsker, from Middle Low German versch. Doublet of fresk, frisk, and fräsch.

parole.significato: a strong, permanent defensive structure; a fortress, a stronghold, a fort
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vesteninge (“fortress”), from vesten (“to fasten, to secure”), from Old Saxon fast (“firm, secure”).
From Old Swedish fanginskaper, from Middle Low German vangenschop, equivalent to fången + -skap.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vangst, from vangen (“to catch”). Doublet of fånga.
From Old Swedish fögha, fögho, föghe (“fitting, ingenious, moderate, slight, little”); like Danish føje from Middle Low German vôge (“appropriate, moderate”), from Old Saxon fogian. Doublet of foga.
From Old Swedish fynster, finster, from Middle Low German vinster, from Latin fenestra. Replaced Native Old Swedish vindögha, from Old Norse vindauga.
From Middle Low German voracht, from Old Saxon, from Proto-West Germanic *firiahtu, from *firi- (“across, through”) + *ahtu (“attention, consideration”). Cognate with German Verachtung.

From Old Swedish forargha, from Middle Low German vorargen, the use affected by German verargen, equivalent to för- + arga or för- + arg + -a. Cognate with Danish forarge, Norwegian Bokmål forarge, Norwegian Nynorsk forarge, forarga and German verargen.
From Old Swedish forbanna, from Middle Low German vorbannen, equivalent to för- + banna. Compare German verbannen.

parole.significato: to reserve, to make a reservation (to reduce the effect of a promise)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German vorbeholden or German vorbehalten, equivalent to för- + behålla. Compare Danish forbeholde.
Compound of för + bi, presumably by Middle Low German vorbi (German vorbei). Cognate with Danish forbi.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorbitteren or German verbittern. By surface analysis, för- + bitter + -a.

parole.significato: to (still) be, to stay (a certain way), to remain
parole.testo: Apocopic form of förbliva, from Middle Low German vorbliven or German verbleiben. Cognate with Danish forblive and Norwegian Bokmål forbli. Equivalent to för- + bli.
From Middle Low German vorborgen (“hidden”), the past participle of vorbergen (“to hide”). Compare German verborgen /verbergen.

From Old Swedish forbætra, from Middle Low German vorbeteren. Cognate with Danish forbedre, Norwegian Bokmål forbedre, Norwegian Nynorsk forbetre, forbetra, German verbessern and Dutch verbeteren. Equivalent to för- + bättra or för + bättre + a.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vordrach. Cognate of German Vertrag.

From Old Swedish fordriva, from Middle Low German vordriven, from Old Saxon fardrīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *fradrīban, equivalent to för- + driva. Cognate with Danish fordrive, Norwegian Bokmål fordrive, Norwegian Nynorsk fordriva, fordrive, Old Norse fordrífa, German vertreiben and English for
Inherited from Old Swedish fordömeliker, from Middle Low German vordōmlik, vordōmelik. By surface analysis, fördöma + -lig. Cognate of Danish fordømmelig.
From Old Swedish forena, förena, from Middle Low German vorenen and German vereinen. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål forene, Danish forene, Dutch verenen. Equivalent to för- + ena.
före + ta. Calque of Middle Low German vornemen. Compare English foretake and German vornehmen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vörvelschen, vorvelschen, from Old Saxon *farfalskōn, from Proto-West Germanic *frafalskōn. By surface analysis, för- + falsk + -a. Cognate of Danish forfalske.

parole.significato: to proceed, to handle, to do (things in a particular manner)
parole.testo: för- + fara, from Old Swedish forfara, from Middle Low German vorvaren, from Old Saxon faran (“to travel, go”), cognate with German verfahren.
From Middle Low German vorvaten (“to compose, write”), equivalent to för- + fatta. Cognate with Danish forfatte, Norwegian Bokmål forfatte, Norwegian Nynorsk forfatte, forfatta and German verfassen.

parole.significato: to dispose (over something), to have access (to something)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vörvö̂gen, vorvö̂gen, vorvogen, equivalent to för- + foga. Compare German verfügen.

parole.significato: to defend (an opinion), to fight for (an opinion)
parole.testo: för- + fäkta, used since 1544, cognate with Danish forfægte, from Middle Low German vorvechten and German verfechten.
From Old Swedish forfæra, from Middle Low German vorvēren, vorvāren, related to fara (“danger”), from Old Saxon *fāra, fār, from Proto-Germanic *fērō (“danger”). Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål forferde.
From Old Swedish forfærliker, from Middle Low German vorvērlik, from vorvēren + -lik, equivalent to förfära + -lig.

parole.significato: to seduce, to attract; to induce someone into a sexual relationship.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorvoren or German verführen. Equivalent to för- + föra.

parole.significato: to mistreat, to disadvantage, to give someone less than they deserve
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German vorvordelen, equivalent to för- + fördela. Cognate of Danish forfordele.

parole.significato: transience (all living things – and even matter itself – inevitably ceasing to exist), decomposition (through death), a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish forgangilse. Calque of Middle Low German vorgenknis, equivalent to förgå (“vanish”) + -else

From Old Swedish forgangliker, from Middle Low German vorgenklik, from vorgān (“expire”), cognate with Danish forgængelig, Norwegian Bokmål forgjengelig, Norwegian Nynorsk forgjengeleg, German vergänglich and Dutch vergankelijk. Equivalent to för- (“fore-”) + gång (“going”) + -lig (“-ly”) or förgå +

parole.significato: to forget; to lose remembrance of
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forgæta, from Middle Low German vorgēten, from Old Saxon fargetan, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan.

parole.significato: to vanish, to pass (away), to cease, to run out, to die
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German vorgan or German vergehen, equivalent to för- + gå. Compare Danish forgå, English forgo.

parole.significato: an abatis, a defense obstacle made by felling trees in a mesh
parole.testo: förhugga + -ning, used in Swedish since 1761, likely inspired by German Verhau. The verb förhugga (obsolete, never listed in SAOL) is known from Old Swedish forhugga, from Middle Low German vorhouwen, cognate with German verhauen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorherden. By surface analysis, för- + härda. Cognate of Danish forhærde, German verhärten.
From Middle Low German vorhonen or German verhöhnen, equivalent to för- + håna. Compare Danish forhåne.
Inherited from Old Swedish forhögia, from Middle Low German vorhogen. By surface analysis, för- + höja.
Inherited from Old Swedish forhøra, from Middle Low German vorhoren. Cognate of German verhören.
Inherited from Old Swedish foriägha, from Middle Low German vorjagen, equivalent to för- + jaga. Cognate of German verjagen. First attested in 1430.

From Old Swedish forklara, from Middle Low German vorklaren, equivalent to för- + klar + -a or för- + klara. Cognate with Danish forklare, Norwegian Bokmål forklare, Norwegian Nynorsk forklara, forklare, forklåra, forklåre, Dutch verklaren, Limburgish verklaore, Afrikaans verklaar and German erkläre
From Middle Low German vorklênen, vorklenen. By surface analysis, för- + klen + -a. Cognate with Danish forkleine, German verkleinern.
Inherited from Old Swedish forkofra, from Middle Low German vorkoveren, from Old French recovrer, from Latin recuperāre. Cognate of French recouvrer.
From Old Swedish forkynna, forkynda, forkunna, from Middle Low German vorkunden. Compare German verkünden, Danish forkynde.
Inherited from Old Swedish forlidhen, from Middle Low German vorlīden. The German word is equivalent to vor- (“before”) affixed to a verb from the root Proto-Germanic *līþaną (“to pass”).
From Old Swedish forlika, from Middle Low German vorliken (“make equal”).

parole.significato: to be wrecked, to go under, to sink (of a ship)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorlisen, vorlêsen (“to lose”), from Old Saxon farliosan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraleusan, from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną. Doublet of förlora (“to lose”). Compare Danish forlise, Norwegian forlise, Dutch verliezen, German verlieren, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍃𐌰𐌽 (fraliusan).

parole.significato: to lose (a competition, fight, or the like)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorloren (German verloren), the past participle of vorlêsen (“to lose”), from Old Saxon farliosan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraleusan, from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną. Doublet of förlisa. Compare Afrikaans verloor.

parole.significato: to deliver (to assist in giving birth)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German vorlosen, equivalent to för- + lossa. Doublet of förlösa.

parole.significato: to get engaged (to agree to marry)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forlova, from Middle Low German vorloven, equivalent to för- + lova. Compare German verloben.

parole.significato: a veil, a curtain (often in religious contexts)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German vorlat. First attested in 1527.

From Old Swedish forlata, from Middle Low German vorlaten (“to leave”), from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną, equivalent to för- + låta. Cognate with Danish forlade, German verlassen, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌻𐌴𐍄𐌰𐌽 (fralētan), English forlet

parole.significato: to deliver (assist (someone) in delivering a baby)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German vorlosen, equivalent to för- + lösa. Doublet of förlossa.
Inherited from Old Swedish formiddelst, from Middle Low German vormiddelst. Cognate of German vermittels, Danish formedelst.
Inherited from Old Swedish formyndarskap, from Middle Low German vormunderschap. By surface analysis, förmyndare + -skap.
From Old Swedish formætin, from Middle Low German vormeten, the past participle of a verb originally meaning "to overestimate" or "to mismeasure". Cognate of German vermessen.

parole.significato: to be capable, be able to
parole.testo: From younger Old Swedish formā, apocopic form of older Old Swedish formāga, formāgha, from Middle Low German vermogen (or German vermögen), equivalent to för- + må. Cognate with Danish formå, Norwegian formå, Old Norse formuga, younger Icelandic fyrirmoga and Dutch vermogen.
From Old Swedish fornidhra, from Middle Low German vornederen. Cognate of Danish fornedre, Dutch vernederen, and German erniedrigen.

From Middle Low German vornemen, compare German vernehmen. Equivalent to för- + nimma (“take”). Although the verb nimma (and by extension this one) originally belonged to the class 4 of strong verbs, it has merged into class 3, possibly analogically to simma.
From Old Swedish fornumstogher (“reasonable”), from Old Swedish fornumst (“reason”), from Middle Low German vornumst (“reason”). Compare förnuft.
From Middle Low German van nōden (“out of necessity”). Compare German vonnöten.
From Old Swedish fornø̄ghia, from Middle Low German vornögen, equivalent to för- + nöja. Attested since 1709. Compare German vergnügen.

From Middle Low German vororsaken and German verursachen, equivalent of för- + orsaka (“to cause”). Cognate with Danish forårsage, Norwegian Bokmål forårsake, Norwegian Nynorsk forårsake, forårsaka and Dutch veroorzaken.

parole.significato: wrong (to treat unjustly), injure, to fail to treat someone with due respect
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German verunrechten.
Inherited from Old Swedish forplikta, from Middle Low German vorplichten. Cognate of German verpflichten, Norwegian Bokmål forplikte.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorplegen or German verpflegen. By surface analysis, för- + pläga. Cognate of Danish forpleje.

parole.significato: to undervalue, to minimize, to belittle, to value less than what it should be
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorringen, equivalent to för- + ringa + -a. Cognate with Danish forringe and Norwegian Bokmål forringe.
Old Swedish forrædheri, likely borrowed from unattested Middle Low German *vorrederie. By surface analysis, förrädare + -eri. Cognate of Danish forræderi, German Verräterei.

parole.significato: to forsake, to sacrifice, to forgo
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forsaka, from Middle Low German vorsaken, from Old Saxon farsakan.

parole.significato: to provide, to equip, to supply
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forsea, from Middle Low German vorsen, equivalent to för- + se.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorschonen or German verschonen. By surface analysis, för- + skona. Cognate of Danish forskåne.
Inherited from Old Swedish forslita, from Middle Low German vorsliten. By surface analysis, för- + slita. Cognate of Danish forslide.
Derived from Middle Low German vorsmechten. By surface analysis, för- + smäkta. Cognate of Danish forsmægte, German verschmachten.
From Old Swedish forsmā (“belittle”), from Middle Low German vorsman. Compare German verschmähen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorsnellen. First attested in 1581.
From Old Swedish forsona, from Middle Low German vorsonen. Equivalent of för- + sona. Cognate with Danish forsone.

parole.significato: to waste (not put to good use)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forspilla, a calque of Middle Low German vorspilden, equivalent to för- + spilla. Compare English forspill.
för- + stoppa, from Old Swedish forstoppa, from Middle Low German vorstoppen. Compare German verstopfen.
Through apocope with umlaut from Old Swedish forstanda, from Middle Low German vörstenden, from Old Saxon farstandan. Cognate with Danish forstå and German verstehen. Equivalent to för- + stå.
From Middle Low German vorstandich, vorstendich, equivalent to förstånd + -ig. Cognate of Danish forstandig, German verständig, Dutch verstandig.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorsumen. Cognate of Danish forsømme, Dutch verzuimen, German versäumen.

parole.significato: to defend (by military, in court, and elsewhere)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forsvara, calque of Middle Low German vorantworden (cf. German verantworten and Dutch verantwoorden), equivalent to för- + svara. Cognate with Danish forsvare, Norwegian Bokmål forsvare, Norwegian Nynorsk forsvara, forsvare.
för- + svinna, ultimately from Middle Low German vorswinden.

parole.significato: to insure; to get an insurance for
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forsækra, from Middle Low German vorsekeren, equivalent of för- + säker + -a or för- + säkra. Cognate with Danish forsikre, Norwegian Bokmål forsikre, Norwegian Nynorsk forsikre, forsikra, Dutch verzekeren and German versichern.
By surface analysis, för- + tro. Borrowed from either Middle Low German vortruwen or German vertrauen. Cognate of Danish fortro and Dutch vertrouwen.
16th century, calque of Middle Low German vordrengen. Equivalent to för- + tränga. The technical use in psychology follows modern German verdrängen. Compare also Danish fortrænge, Dutch verdringen.

From Old Swedish fortvifla, from Middle Low German vortwivelen, equivalent to för- + tvivla. Cognate with Danish fortvivle, Norwegian Bokmål fortvile, Norwegian Nynorsk fortvila, Norwegian Nynorsk fortvile and German verzweifeln.

From Old Swedish fortælia, from Middle Low German vortellen. Cognate with Danish fortælle, Norwegian Bokmål fortelle, Norwegian Nynorsk fortelje, fortelja, Dutch vertellen, Low German vertellen, regional German verzählen. Equivalent to för- + tälja.

parole.significato: to eat or drink, to consume
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fortæra, from Middle Low German vorteren (cognate of German verzehren). Equivalent to för- + tära (cognate with English tear), from Proto-Germanic *teraną.

parole.significato: to delay, to linger, to postpone
parole.testo: för- + töva, cognate with Old Swedish fortöva, from Middle Low German vortoven (delay, wait, obstruct)

parole.significato: to surprise and cause to wonder; confound
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forundra, calque of Middle Low German vorwunderen, equivalent to för- (“en-”) + undra (“wonder”). Compare German verwundern.

parole.significato: to turn, to transform, to convert (especially through magic, or figuratively as if through magic)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish forvandla, from Middle Low German vorwandelen, equivalent to för- (“en-”) + vandla (“change, transform (obsolete)”). Compare Danish forvandle, German verwandeln.

From Old Swedish forvara, from Middle Low German vorwaren. Cognate with Danish forvare, Norwegian Bokmål forvare, Norwegian Nynorsk forvare, forvara, Middle Dutch verwaren and German verwahren. Equivalent to för- + vara (“last”).
From Old Swedish forværka, from Middle Low German vorwerken, equivalent to för- + verka. First attested in the late 13th century. Cognate with Danish forvirke, German verwirken.
Inherited from Old Swedish forvisa, from Middle Low German vorwisen, equivalent to för- + visa. Cognate of German verweisen.
Inherited from Old Swedish forvissa, from Middle Low German vorwissen.
Inherited from Old Swedish forvænda, from Middle Low German vorwenden. Cognate of German verwenden (“turn away”).

parole.significato: honor, present someone with an award
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German voreren. By surface analysis, för- + ära. Cognate of German verehren.

parole.significato: to team up, to band together (against someone or something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German gaden.
From Middle Low German gaffel, gaffele, from Old Saxon gavala, gafila, from Proto-West Germanic *gabulu, possibly from Celtic.

parole.significato: a grid, a lattice, bars; a pattern like XXX or ||| formed by several long, more-or-less rigid objects
parole.testo: From Old Swedish galdror, probably from Middle Low German gaddere (from whence German Gitter).
From Middle Low German gans, gansch, from Middle High German ganz, from Old High German ganz, from Proto-West Germanic *gant.
From Middle Low German gerwen, from Old Saxon gerwian, from Proto-West Germanic *garwijan, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk garva (“tan”) and Danish garve (“tan”). (laugh)
Borrowed from Middle Low German gelik, from Old Saxon gilīk, from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.
From Middle Low German gemak, cognate with German Gemach. Originally in the sense of comfort, ease, calmness. Used in the sense of a room since 1627.

Borrowed from Middle Low German gemēn, from Old Saxon gimeni, from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz. Cognate with English mean, German gemein, Dutch gemeen, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (gamains) and Latin communis.

parole.significato: a journeyman (tradesman who has served an apprenticeship)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German geselle, from Old Saxon gisellio, from Proto-Germanic *gasaljô.
Inherited from Old Swedish glas, from Middle Low German glas, from Old Saxon glas.

From Old Swedish glaven (glaffwin, glawan) n, m, glavene n, variant of glävia, glafwia, glafwa f, from Middle Low German glave, gleve, glevie, obl. & pl. glaven, from Old French glaive (“lance,”) from Latin gladius (“sword”); possibly of Celtic origin. Compare Danish glavind, Icelandic glefja, Engli

parole.significato: to move smoothly along a surface; to slide, to slip, to glide, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German glīden, from Old Saxon glīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰleydʰ-.

parole.significato: having a voracious appetite, insatiable, greedy
parole.testo: From Middle Low German glupesch, related to German glupschen. Equivalent to glupa + -sk. See also Danish glubsk.
From Middle Low German grēve, from Old Saxon grāvio, from Proto-West Germanic *garāfijō. Cognate to Danish greve and English reeve.

parole.significato: county, the domain of a count (nobleman)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish grevaskap, from Middle Low German greveschap. By surface analysis, greve + -skap.
From Middle Low German krōde, krode, from Old Saxon *kroda, from Proto-West Germanic *krodu (“toad”) of origin unknown, related to German Kröte. Compare dialectal Norwegian Nynorsk gro (“toad”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German *groll, grull (“grudge”), from Old Saxon *grullio, from Proto-West Germanic *grulljō.

parole.significato: coarse; composed of relatively large particles or pieces
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grof.
From Middle Low German gruveln and German grübeln. Doublet of gräva.
From Old Swedish grundeliker, equivalent to grund + -lig. Borrowed from Middle Low German grundlik. Compare German gründlich and English groundly.
From Old Swedish grus, from Middle Low German grus, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *greutą (“grit”).

parole.significato: mine (place from which ore is extracted)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grôve, from Proto-Germanic *grōbō (“groove, furrow”). The modern sense is a semantic loan from German Grube, from the same Germanic etymon.
Inherited from Old Swedish gruveliker, from Middle Low German grūwelik. Compare German greulich, Dutch gruwelijk.
From Middle Low German grellen (“to shout at, antagonize”).

parole.significato: lasting bitterness along with anger or frustration, (sometimes) resentment
parole.testo: From Middle Low German gremenisse.

Borrowed from Middle Low German grootmündig (“bigmouthed”). By surface analysis, gröt (“porridge”) + myndig (“authoritative”). According to SO attested since 1669. Compare Danish grødmyndig, Low German grootmödig, Dutch grootmond.
Borrowed from Middle Low German gokelen, influenced by Latin joculor. Cognate of German gaukeln, Danish gøgle. Doublet of jonglera.
Inherited from Old Swedish gæk (“jester; fool”), from Middle Low German geck. Cognate of Danish gæk, Dutch gek, German Geck. Possibly related to English geek.
Old Swedish gäkka, from Middle Low German gecken and geck.

parole.significato: only used in hack i häl (“hot on someone's heels, (snapping) at someone's heels”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German or German Hacke (“heel”). Probably related to Swedish hake (“hook”).

parole.significato: a pick, pickaxe; a tool used to hack
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish hakka, likely borrowed from Middle Low German hacken. Cognate with Dutch hakken, German hacken. Senses "amount of money" and "low-rank cards" influenced by Middle Low German hacke (“mincemeat”), with the implication that minced meat is of low value.

From Old Swedish haffa, from Middle Low German haffen (“to handle, treat by hand”), related to Middle Low German haven (“to have, hold”) and Middle Low German hebben (“to have”). Compare also Middle High German haben (“to have, grab, seize”).

parole.significato: to reel, to haul (pull on something so as to bring more and more of it to oneself, often in order to bring in things at…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German halen, from Old Saxon halon.
From Middle Low German halveren or German halbieren, equivalent to halv + -era.
From Middle Low German hanteren.
From Middle Low German hantwerk from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to hand (“hand”) + verk (“work”). Cognate with Dutch handwerk, German Handwerk, English handwork.

parole.significato: hurry, rush; to move (or act) quickly, and possibly cutting corners to finish quickly
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hasten.
Equivalent to hem + söka, from Old Swedish hemsøkning, from Middle Low German heimsoken. Cognate of Middle High German heimsuochen, German heimsuchen, Danish hjemsøge, Icelandic heimsækja.

parole.significato: Mr., Mister, gentleman, sir (respectful term of address or title for an adult male)
parole.testo: Clipping of herre. Likely influenced by Middle Low German her and German Herr.

From Old Swedish hitza, hissa, from Middle Low German hitzen, hissen, likely originating from some interjection given to dogs (eg. hiss). Compare Danish hidse, Norwegian hissa, Dutch hitsen (particularly aanhitsen, ophitsen), Middle High German hessen. Certain senses influenced by German hetzen.
From Old Swedish hingist, hingest, hengist, from Middle Low German hengest, hengst, hingest, hingst.

Uncertain. Arguably from Middle Low German henneke, hinke, from Hinrik. If so, doublet of Henke. Compare similar shift in meaning from personal name to device in German Heinz, Dietrich and English jack. Compare Finnish hinkalo (“grain bin”).

parole.significato: court; the people surrounding a ruler, such as a monarch or an emperor; the accommodation of a monarch
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hof, from Old Saxon hof. Cognate with German Hof, Danish hof.

parole.significato: simple but hearty traditional everyday food
parole.testo: From Middle Low German husmannskost, from husmann (“crofter, day laborer”) + kost (“food”), compare Swedish husman + kost.
From Middle Low German hovetstol. Compare with Danish hovedstol.
From Middle Low German hüchelen, further origin disputed. Cognate of Danish hykle, and most likely with German heucheln and Dutch huichelen.

parole.significato: a rent; what is paid in order to rent something
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hüre, from Old Saxon huria.
Cognate with Danish høvl, Norwegian Bokmål høvel, German Hobel, based on Middle Low German hovel, of uncertain origin. Attested in Swedish from 1548.
Borrowed from Middle Low German helen. Same root word as etymology 1. Doublet of hölja. Cognate of Danish hæle, German hehlen, Dutch helen (“to fence”).

parole.significato: stove, heater; an enclosed space in which fuel (usually wood) is burned to provide heating, usually for cooking
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hærþer, from Middle Low German herd, from Old Saxon heorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *herþ.

Borrowed from Middle Low German herkomst, herkumpst. Compare similarly borrowed ankomst (“arrival”) and tillkomst (“coming into existence, creation”). The second element -komst is from Proto-Germanic *kumþiz, but is not a native Swedish formation, rather a borrowing of the Middle Low German suffix.
From Old Swedish hætsker, from Middle Low German hetisch or hatisch. Compare Danish hadsk. Doublet of hatisk.

parole.significato: to mock, deride, make fun of
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hônen, from Old Saxon hōnian, from Proto-West Germanic *haunijan (“to humiliate”). Compare Danish håne.
Originally borrowed from Middle Low German hufte. Displaced Old Swedish miædhm, from Old Norse mjǫðm.
From Old Swedish høghfærdh, from Middle Low German hochvart. Equivalent to hög (“pride”) + färd (“manner”). Cognate of German Hoffart, Dutch hovaard.

From Middle Low German hȫker (“peddler”), perhaps from Old High German huchan (“to crouch, sit bent forward”), from Proto-Germanic *hūkan- (“to squat”), from *hūkkan-, back-formed from the iterative *huk(k)ōn-, from Proto-Indo-European *kuk-néh₂, from *kewk- (“to curve, bend”) (also the source of En

From Old Swedish høvitzman, probably from older huvuþsmaþer, from Middle Low German hövetsman. Doublet of huvudman. Compare Icelandic höfuðsmaður, German Hauptmann, English headsman. See also hövding.
From Middle Low German van unnôden.
From Middle Low German idel (“empty, pure, vain”). Compare English idle (“empty, vacant”), German eidel (“empty, vain”).

parole.significato: to hurry, to speed (move quickly and hurriedly)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ila, from Middle Low German īlen, from Proto-West Germanic *īlijan (“to make haste, hasten”).
From Middle Low German inbilden, equivalent to German einbilden. The German word is perhaps from Latin imaginor. Compare Danish indbilde.
Derived from Middle Low German ingever.
From Middle Low German inkrechten (“to take with force”). Compare Dutch kracht (“force”).

From Old Swedish innehald, from Middle Low German inhold or German Inhalt, equivalent of inne + håll. Cognate with Danish indhold (whence Norwegian Bokmål innhold and Norwegian Nynorsk innhald), Low German Inholt, Dutch inhoud, Afrikaans inhoud, Limburgish inhaadj, Yiddish אינהאַלט (inhalt), West Fr
Borrowed from Middle Low German inrümen. By surface analysis, in + rymma. Compare German einräumen.

parole.significato: to attest, to certify, to confirm
parole.testo: From Middle Low German intügen. Cognate with German einzeugen.

parole.significato: internal (pertaining to the inside of the body)
parole.testo: in + -värtes. From Old Swedish invärtis, from Middle Low German inwerdes, same as English inwards (“towards the inside”).

From Middle Low German īwer, possibly originally from Proto-West Germanic *aibr, from Proto-Germanic *aibraz (“sharp, bitter, vehement, dire, violent”, adj.). Cognate with Danish iver, Norwegian Bokmål iver, Norwegian Nynorsk iver, German Eifer, Luxembourgish Äifer, Dutch ijver and Afrikaans ywer.

parole.significato: a jacket, a doublet, a jerkin
parole.testo: From Middle Low German jacke, from French jaque, from Old French jacque.
From Late Old Swedish iakt, from Early Old Swedish iækt, from Middle Low German jacht.

parole.significato: to do pelvic thrusts (during sex or otherwise), to hump
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German jücken, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *jukkjan.
From Old Swedish iuþe, from Middle Low German jude, from Old Saxon judo, from Latin judæus, from Ancient Greek ἰουδαῖος (ioudaîos). Cognate with Icelandic júði.

parole.significato: noise like from mourning or pain; lamentation, whimpering, wailing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish iæmber, from Middle Low German jammer, ultimately onomatopoeic. Cognate of German Jammer, English yammer.
Borrowed from Middle Low German kabuse. Cognate with English caboose.
Inherited from Old Swedish kayuta, from Middle Low German kajūte. Cognate of German Kajüte, Dutch kajuit. Exact relationship with French cahute unclear.
From Old Swedish kalker, from Middle Low German kalk, from Latin calx.
From Middle Low German kanīn, konīn, from Old French connin, connil, from Latin cuniculus.
Inherited from Old Swedish kapun, from Middle Low German kappūn, from Old French capun, capon, from Latin cāpō. Cognate of Italian cappone, French chapon, German Kapaun, Dutch kapoen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German karduse, kartuse, from French cartouche, from Italian cartoccio. Cognate of Danish kardus, Dutch kardoes. Doublet of kartesch and kartusch.
From Middle Low German karpe, from Medieval Latin carpa, of Germanic, but ultimately non-Indo-European origin; see Old High German karpho.
Derived from Middle Low German keef, further origin disputed.

parole.significato: chain (a series of interconnected rings or links)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish kædhe, kædhia, from Middle Low German kede (from kedene), from Latin catēna. Cognate of French chaîne, English chain, German Kette, Dutch keten.
From Middle Low German kîken.
Borrowed from Middle Low German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kīnaną (“to split, crack open”).

From older kirs, kers + kål (“cabbage”). The former is originally from Middle Low German gerse (cf. German Giersch), but was confused (either in Swedish or Low German itself) with unrelated kerse (“cress”).

parole.significato: a hinged flap able to be raised and lowered
parole.testo: Probably related to klapp, itself borrowed from Middle Low German klap, from Old Saxon klappōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klappōn (“to strike, clap, make a loud sound”).

parole.significato: to complain (whether in a whiny way or not)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klagha, borrowed from Middle Low German klagen, from Old Saxon klagon, from Proto-West Germanic *klagōn (“to lament, complain”).
From Middle Low German klar, from Latin clarus (“bright, clear”).

Inherited from Old Swedish klenodh, klenat, klenät, klenot, kleenodh, clenodh, clenod, clenodum, from Middle Low German klēnade, klēnode, kleinode, from kleine, klene. Cognate of Dutch kleinood, German Kleinod. See also Norwegian klenodium, Latin clenōdium. Doublet of klenät.
From Old Swedish klenäthe, from Middle Low German klēnade, klēnode, kleinode. Doublet of klenod.
