From Old Swedish klinga, from Middle Low German klingen, from Old Saxon klingen, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą. Cognate with English clink.

parole.significato: a cliff, a rock (a cliff, or a rock formation with a cliff or cliffs (a steep rock formation, put differently) – compar…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German klippe, related to klif (“cliff, rock”), from Old Saxon *klif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.

parole.significato: a solid (large) ball, often harder than a boll
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klōt, from Middle Low German klôt, from Old Saxon *klōt, from Proto-Germanic *klautaz. Cognate of German Kloß, English cleat, Dutch kloot. Compare with origin for klut.
Deverbal from klottra. From Middle Low German klūteren.
Probably from Middle Low German kluteren. Likely cognate of Danish kludre (“to bungle”). Possibly from the same root as kloss, klot, or klut. Compare with kludda.
Borrowed from Middle Low German klumpe, from Old Saxon *klumpo, from Proto-Germanic *klumpô.
From Old Swedish klēver, from Middle Low German klêver, via Old Saxon from Proto-West Germanic *klaibrā. Cognate of Danish kløver, English clover. In sense 2, semantic loan from French trèfle.
From Middle Low German knap, whence also German knapp, Danish knap. Further cognate with Dutch knap. Compare also Danish næppe (“hardly at all”).

parole.significato: a (foot) soldier (especially in the medieval and early modern period)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German knecht, from Old Saxon kneht, from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.

parole.significato: a trick (non-obvious, often clever way to accomplish something)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German knep. Cognate of Danish kneb. Compare also recent German Kniff. Related to the verb knipa (“squeeze”). Doublet of knip, knippe, and knippa.

parole.significato: to pinch, to squeeze (often two body parts against each other)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German knīpen, from Proto-Germanic *knīpaną (“to pinch”).
From Middle Low German knōp (“knot”), probably via Old Saxon from a variant of Proto-Germanic *knappô (“knob, lump”), one of several kn- words related to *knuttô (“knot”). Compare Dutch knoop.
Borrowed from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch knoppe; probably via Old Saxon from a variant of Proto-Germanic *knappô (“knob, lump”), perhaps related to *knappō (“knob, boy”).
From Middle Low German knuffen or German knuffen.

parole.significato: a chef, a cook (person who prepares food for a living)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kok, kock, from Old Saxon kok, from Proto-West Germanic *kok, from Latin coquus.
From Middle Low German koker. Compare German Köcher, Old English cocer.

parole.significato: to boil (turn from liquid into gas by creating gas bubbles throughout the liquid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kôken, from Old Saxon *kokōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn.

parole.significato: an art (a liberal art, to make artworks)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish konst, from Middle Low German kunst, from the verb kunnen (“to know”), from Old Saxon kunnan.

parole.significato: an artist (person who creates works of art (in the usual sense, like for example a painter or sculptor))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kunstener; see konst (“art”) for more on the root. Attested since 1667.

Since late 16th century, borrowed from Middle Low German kontôr, komtôr, komptor (“commercial branch; writing room; counting desk/table”), from Middle Dutch contoor, contoir, comptoir, from Middle French contoir, comptoir, from conter, compter (“to count”) + -oir (instrument suffix).

parole.significato: a leash (for dogs or the like)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German koppel, from Latin cōpula.

Inherited from Old Swedish kora, from Middle Low German koren. Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål kåre. From Proto-Germanic *kuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-. Compare origin of kurfurste, tjusa, villkor.
From Middle Low German kort, from Old Saxon *kurt, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, an early borrowing from Latin curtus. Cognate with German kurz, Dutch kort, Danish kort and Norwegian Bokmål kort.

parole.significato: vertebra; an element of the backbone
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kota (“bone, knot”), from Middle Low German kote (“claw, hoof”), for which see Dutch koot (“phalanx”).
From Middle Low German krampe (whence Norwegian krampe and Danish krampe), from Old Saxon krampo, from Proto-Germanic *krampō, from Proto-Indo-European *grem-.
From Middle Low German kran, from krane (“crane”), from Old Saxon *krano, from Proto-West Germanic *kranō.
Inherited from Old Swedish krasse, from Middle Low German karse, from Proto-West Germanic *krassjā. Cognate with German Kresse, French cresson.
Borrowed from Middle Low German krîch. Unlike Norwegian and Danish krig, the Swedish word has neutrum gender like Faroese kríggj.
From Old Swedish kristinhet, from Middle Low German kristenheit, equivalent to kristen + -het. Compare Danish kristenhed, German Christenheit.
From Middle Low German krite, from Latin creta. The credit sense is from marking credit with a piece of chalk.

parole.significato: a (more rustic) premise where alcohol is sold and consumed; a pub, (except often not as strong in tone) a tavern
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krogher, from Middle Low German krôch, from Proto-Germanic *kranhō (“corner”), which according to Kroonen could be related to *kringaną (“to turn, yield”). However, it could otherwise be from Proto-Germanic *kragan- (“throat”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ-, which could

parole.significato: to crush; to press or bruise between two hard bodies until the point of breaking
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krossa, krosa, krusa, probably from Middle Low German krossen (“to break”).

parole.significato: a pot (container, often made of clay, for example for growing a plant in (blomkruka))
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle Low German krûke, from Old Saxon krūka, from Proto-West Germanic *krūkā (“pot, pitcher”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European root shared with Old Armenian կարաս (karas, “pitcher, large jar”), Ancient Greek κρωσσός (krōssós, “pitcher”), but the phonetics ar
From Middle Low German krum, from Old Saxon krumb, from Proto-West Germanic *krump, from Proto-Germanic *krumpaz.

Inherited from Old Swedish krusa, from Middle Low German krûsen, related with Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”). Further origin uncertain. Possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of
From Middle Low German krusbere (“gooseberry”).

Borrowed and clipped from Middle Low German büssenkrūt, bussenkrût (“gunpowder”), from büsse (“rifle”) + krût (“spice, herb”), from Old Saxon krūd, from Proto-West Germanic *krūd (“herb, plant”). Doublet of krydda.

parole.significato: a crutch (device to assist in motion)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krykkia, from Middle Low German krucke, krocke, krücke, from Old Saxon krukka, from Proto-West Germanic *krukkju, from Proto-Germanic *krukjō (whence also English crutch), from Proto-Indo-European *grewg-.
From Middle Low German krūde (“herb”). Doublet of krut.

parole.significato: The letter "X" in the Swedish spelling alphabet; an alternative spelling word for Xerxes
parole.testo: From Middle Low German krü̂ze, from Old Saxon krūci; ultimately from Latin crux. Sense 5 from the 1-X-2 (Home-Tie-Away) system commonly found on Swedish betting coupons.

parole.significato: a monger, a merchant, (when operating a shop) a shopkeeper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German krēmer. Cognate of German Krämer, Danish kræmmer and Norwegian Nynorsk kremmar. By surface analysis, kräma + -are.

parole.significato: to attack or violate someone's personal honor (with words or actions); to violate, to disrespect, to insult, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krænkia, from Middle Low German krenken, from Old Saxon *krenkian, from Proto-West Germanic *krankijan. Cognate of German kränken, Dutch krenken, Danish krænke, Norwegian krenke, Icelandic krenkja.

From Old Swedish kompan, kumpan, kompon, from Middle Low German kumpān, from Old French compain, compaing, from Late Latin compāniō (literally “he with whom one shares one's bread”), from com- + pānis (with + bread). Cognate of German Kumpan, Kumpel, Icelandic kumpánn, kompánn, Polish kompan. Double
From Old Swedish kunskaper, from Middle Low German kuntschap, from kunt (“known”) suffixed with -schap. Equivalent to kunna + -skap. Compare German Kenntnis and German Kundschaft.
Inherited from Old Swedish kupa (“bowl”), likely from Middle Low German kupe (“bowl; barrel”), from Latin cūpa (“barrel”). Doublet of kupol.

parole.significato: a small shed or roof, a shelter or sentry-box
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kūr, related to kūren (origin of German kauern and English cower), according to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, bend”), see also Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“shell, pod”).

parole.significato: a style of decorative floral painting with large, fantastical flowers, especially associated with Dalecarlia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German körvitz, itself borrowed from Middle High German kürbiz, from Old High German kurbiz, from Proto-West Germanic *kurbit.
Likely borrowed from Middle Low German qualm. Cognate with German Qualm, Dutch kwalm.
Derived from Middle Low German quit, from Old French quitte, from Medieval Latin quitus, from Latin quiētus.

parole.significato: receipt (written acknowledgement of payment, delivery, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kvittancia, from Middle Low German quitancie, from Medieval Latin quitantia, from Latin quietantia. Cognate of English quittance, German Quittanz, French quittance, Italian quietanza.

parole.significato: a receipt (written acknowledgement of the goods purchased and the sum paid)
parole.testo: Ellipsis of kvittobrev, from Middle Low German quitebrêf, from quiten (“to liberate; to confirm a transaction”) + bref (“letter”). See German quittieren (“to sign a receipt”) + Brief (“letter”) for more on the components.

parole.significato: to quell, to suppress, to put down
parole.testo: From Middle Low German quessen, quetsen, quetten. Cognate of German quetschen, Danish kvæsse, kvæste. Arguably related to English quash, Dutch kwetsen.

From Middle Low German küper, from Middle Low German kupe (“cask”). Compare English cooper, Dutch kuiper (“cooper”), Danish kyper (“cellarer”), German Küfer (“cellarman”). See also German Kellner (“waiter”).
From Old Swedish kysker, from Middle Low German kūsch, ultimately from Latin conscius. Cognate with Norwegian and Danish kysk, German keusch.

From Old Swedish kæke, probably borrowed from Middle Low German kêke, from Old Saxon *kioka, from Proto-West Germanic *keukā. Cognate with Danish kiæge, Norwegian kjake, English choke, cheek (from Old English ċēoce (“jaw”)).

Inherited from Old Swedish kæmpe, from Middle Low German kempe, from Old Saxon kempio, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“battlefield”). Cognate of Norwegian kjempe, Danish kæmpe, German Kämpe. Compare English champion.
From Middle Low German ketter, from Ancient Greek καθαρός (katharós, “pure”). Compare Danish kætter, Dutch ketter, German Ketzer, English Cathar.
From Old Swedish kätteri, from Middle Low German ketterie, equivalent to kättare + -eri. Compare Danish kætteri, German Ketzerei.

parole.significato: a (wooden) house in poor condition, a shack, a ramshackle house
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish kaker, from Middle Low German kāk, a form of “pillory”, a pole where different punishments were carried out, probably ultimately from the root of kägla (“pin, cone”). Old Swedish kaker, also denoted the foundation of the pole, usually a raised platform, which also appears

parole.significato: a small bowl with a handle
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kouwese. Cognate with Lithuanian káušas, Russian ковш (kovš), dialectal Danish kovse (“pot”) and, probably, Norwegian Nynorsk koks. Synonymous, but not related to koxa.

parole.significato: a goahti (traditional dwelling of the Sami people)
parole.testo: From a confluence of: # Middle Low German kāte, kōte (“hut”), from Old Saxon *kota, from Proto-West Germanic *kotā, from Proto-Germanic *kutǭ ~ *kutą (“stall, tent”); compare German Kate. # A derivative of Proto-Samic *koatē, from Proto-Uralic *kota; compare Southern Sami gåetie. Whether and how the

From Old Swedish kökia, borrowed from Middle Low German köke, koke, kokene, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna (“kitchen; cuisine”), from coquō (“to cook”), from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”). Replaced native stekarehus/stekarahus and eldhus, from which came the switc
From Old Swedish kirsebær, from Middle Low German kersebere. Cognate with Ancient Greek κερασός (kerasós).

parole.significato: a (sac-shaped or tubular) gland or filtering organ (like a lymph node)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kirtel, of disputed origin, possibly from Middle Low German *kertele, metathetic form of kretele. Cognate with Danish kirtel, Norwegian Bokmål kjertel and Norwegian Nynorsk kjertel.

From Old Swedish kirvil, kyrvil, from Middle Low German kervele, kervelde, from Latin caerefolium, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon), from χαίρω (khaírō, “to enjoy”) + φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).
From Middle Low German lak. Cognate of English leak. Doublet of läcka.
Borrowed from Middle Low German lâke (“brine; standing water”), from Old Saxon *laca, from Proto-West Germanic *laku (“steam, pool”).
From Middle Low German last, from the verb lāden (“to load”), from Old Saxon hladan.
Derived from Middle Low German lāt. Doublet of låt. Compare origin of grannlåt.

parole.significato: to accompany (someone) and show the way (to some place); to guide (someone)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German leitsagen, from Old Saxon lēda (“way”) (see ledian (“to lead”)) + seggian (“to say”), originally "show the way."

parole.significato: laity (people who are not members of the clergy)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lekman, from Middle Low German lekmann, the first compound from Latin laicus (“lay”). Compare Danish lægmand and Icelandic leikmaðr.
Related to liv (“life”). May be from Middle Low German leven. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk leven (“noise”).

parole.significato: to deliver (transport something on someone's behalf)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish leverera, from Middle Low German leverēren, from French livrer, from Latin liberare. First attested in 1506.

Inherited from Old Swedish lindormber, from Middle Low German lindworm, from Proto-Germanic *linþawurmiz. Cognate of Old Norse linnormr. By surface analysis, a compound of orm (“serpent”) and a word of disputed origin, arguably meaning "soft" or "pliable". Compare Old Norse linnr (“snake, serpent”)

Inherited from Old Swedish linne, from Middle Low German linne. Doublet of lin. Arguably a back-formation by misinterpreting archaic linnet n (adjective), from linnen c (adjective), as a noun. See Proto-West Germanic *līnīn.

parole.significato: to cry (often over something relatively insignificant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lipen, from lipe (“lip”).

parole.significato: lispound (unit of weight equal to about 8.5 kilograms)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish lifspund, from Middle Low German livespunt. Cognate of English lispound, Danish lispund, German Liespfund.

parole.significato: a long, thin strip (of wood (or metal or the like), to conceal a joint (or for isolation or decoration), like for examp…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lista, probably from Middle Low German lîste, from Old Saxon *līsta, from Proto-West Germanic *līstā, from Proto-Germanic *līstǭ. Cognate with Danish liste, Icelandic lista.

parole.significato: a plumb bob, a plummet, a weight (hanging)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lodh, from Middle Low German lot, from Old Saxon lōd, from Proto-West Germanic *laud.

parole.significato: a race (running competition or (in an extended sense) other speed competition, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lop, from Middle Low German lôp, from Old Saxon hlōpan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną. Related to the verb löpa, corresponding to German laufen and English leap.

parole.significato: to loosen ((from) something that binds or blocks, completely or partially)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lössa, from Middle Low German lossen, derived from the adjective los (“loose”), from Old Saxon lōs, from Proto-West Germanic *laus.
Ellipsis of lotsman, from Middle Low German lōtsman, from Middle English lodesman (“pilot”). Cognate with English lode (“waterway”), German Lotse, Dutch loods.
From Middle Low German lunte (“fuse”). Cognate with English lunt, German Lunte (“fuse”), and Danish lunte (“fuse”).

parole.significato: to trick, to fool, to deceive, to lure
parole.testo: From Middle Low German luren. Cognate with English lour.
From Middle Low German lute
From Middle Low German lûtteren, from Proto-Germanic *hlūtraz. Literal sense attested since 1541, figurative sense attested since 1756. Cognate of German läutern, Danish luttre, Norwegian luttre.

Borrowed from Middle Low German lucke, gelucke. According to the OED, it may be related to the source of English lock (compare Proto-Germanic *lūkaną (“to close, to shut”)). Compare Danish and Norwegian Bokmål lykke, and Norwegian Nynorsk lukke f. Compare also English luck, German Glück, Yiddish גלי
From Old Swedish lykkosamber, from Middle Low German lucksam, luckesam, equivalent to lycka + -o- + -sam.
From Middle Low German lückesālich (“lucky, happy”), equivalent to lycka + salig (both of which are also Middle Low German borrowings). Cognate of Danish lyksalig and German glückselig.
From Old Swedish lykta, from Middle Low German luchte, ultimately derived from Old High German and Old Saxon lioht (“light”). Cognate with Danish lygte, Norwegian lykt.
Borrowed from Middle Low German lecker. Compare Icelandic lekker.

parole.significato: timely, well-timed, fitting, suitable; happening at the right time or occasion
parole.testo: läge (“situation”) + -lig, Old Swedish läghliker, from Middle Low German legelik.

parole.significato: politeness, kind word (mild but firm attempt to influence a person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German limpe. Compare German Glimpf, Old English ġelimpan, ġelimp.
From Old Swedish län, from Middle Low German lēn and from late Old Norse lén, whence also Danish len, Norwegian len, Icelandic lén, Faroese len. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laihną "loan, fief".

parole.significato: a boom, a floating barrier for oil spill containment
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lensen. Cognate of Dutch lenzen.

parole.significato: homework (work that is done at home)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lexe, from Old Saxon lekzia, from Latin lectio.
From Old Swedish lada, from Middle Low German lade (“box, chest”). Cognate with Old English laþe, Old Norse hlaða (“barn, storehouse”), German Lade.
From Old Swedish langsamber, from Middle Low German lanksam, lanksum, from Old Saxon langsam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam (“lengthy, long-lasting”). Equivalent to lång + -sam.
Old Swedish lödha, from Middle Low German lôten (Modern German löten).
Inherited from Old Swedish løþogher, from Middle Low German lōdich. Cognate German -lötig, Norwegian Bokmål lødig, and English lot (“historical unit of weight”).

parole.significato: To move (slightly) a big, heavy or otherwise difficult-to-move object.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German maken, from Old Saxon makōn. Compare German machen.
From Old Swedish makt, from Middle Low German macht, from Old Saxon maht, from Proto-West Germanic *mahti, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz. Compare mäktig.

parole.significato: a guenon (Old World monkey of the genus Cercopithecus)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German merkatte. Cf. German Meerkatze, Dutch meerkat.
From Middle Low German marschalk, from Old Saxon *marhskalk, from Proto-West Germanic *marhaskalk, from *marh (“horse”) + *skalk (“servant”).

Inherited from Old Swedish marsvin (“porpoise”), from Middle Low German mersvīn and German Meerschwein, from Old High German meriswīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mariswīn, from Proto-Germanic *mariswīną; equivalent too Meer (“sea”) + Schwein (“pig”). First attested in 1538. Guinea pig sense borrowed
From Middle Low German matschopie or Dutch maatschappij. Cognate of English mateship.
From Middle Low German mast, from Old Saxon *mast, from Proto-West Germanic *mast.
From Old Swedish matta, from Middle Low German matte, from Latin matta, probably from Punic or Phoenician.
From Old Swedish meth beradho modhe, from Middle Low German mit berādenem mōde.

Known from Old Swedish midhel, middel, medhel, from Middle Low German middel, from Old Saxon middil, from Proto-Germanic *midlą. Same as German Mittel and English middle. parole.significato: but; introducing a clause that contrasts with the preceding clause, sentence or common belief.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish men, from Middle Low German men, man (“but, only”), probably from Old Saxon niwan (itself from components related to nej (“no”) and van- (“mis-, un-”)), with original connotation "not lacking"; possibly under the influence of Old Swedish men (“while, during”) (modern Swedish medan,

parole.significato: to mean; to convey, or to want to convey
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mena, from Middle Low German mēnen, meinen (compare Icelandic meina, Danish mene), from Old Saxon mēnian, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *mein-.

parole.significato: a tit (genus Parus), a small bird
parole.testo: From Middle Low German mêse, meise, from Old Saxon mēsa, from Proto-West Germanic *maisā, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ. Cognate to Norwegian Bokmål meis, meise and Norwegian Nynorsk meis, meise.
Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Cognate of German Mühe (“effort”).

parole.significato: arson; the crime of setting fire to something in order to cause damage
parole.testo: Compound of mord (“murder”) + brand (“fire”). Inherited from Old Swedish mordhbrander (mid-15th c.), possibly after Middle Low German mortbrant. Compare German Mordbrand. Originally only referring to a type of murder, today it refers to general arson.
Borrowed from Middle Low German môrian, likely from Latin Maurītānus, from Maurus. Cognate of Dutch moriaan and possibly Spanish moreno. Compare origin of mor (“Moor”), mauretanier.
From Old Swedish mororot, moro rot, calque of Middle Low German morwortel (“carrot”), from more + wortel. Cf. German Möhre.
Probably from Middle Low German mucken (“to grouse, to grumble”), of onomatopoeic origin.
From Old Swedish morbär via dissimilation. Originally a borrowing of Middle Low German môrbēre, from Old Saxon *mōrberi, from Proto-West Germanic *mōrubaʀi.
Inherited from Old Swedish mumbla, from Middle Low German mummelen, originally onomatopoeic. Compare German mümmeln, Dutch mompelen, English mumble.
Borrowed from Middle Low German mussel, mussele, muschel, muschele, from Latin musculus. Cognate of Dutch mossel, German Muschel, English mussel, Danish musling. Doublet of muskel.

parole.significato: A mosquito (small flying insect of the family Culicidae, known for biting and sucking blood).
parole.testo: From Middle Low German mügge, from Old Saxon muggia, from Proto-West Germanic *muggjā, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō, *mujan, from Proto-Indo-European *mu (“fly”), *mew-. Cognates with Norwegian mygg, Icelandic mý, Danish myg, Old English myċġ, myċġe (whence Middle English migge, English midge); Old Hi

parole.significato: having reached the age of majority
parole.testo: From Old Swedish myndogher, from Middle Low German mündich.

parole.significato: a mutiny (organized rebellion, especially by seamen)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German muterie. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk mytteri
From Old Swedish mæktogher, borrowed from Middle Low German mechtich, from Old Saxon mahtig, equivalent to makt + -ig. Cognate with Norwegian mektig, Danish mægtig.
Inherited from Old Swedish mängia, from Middle Low German mengen. Cognate of Danish mænge, English ming. Doublet of handgemäng.

parole.significato: Master, an older title of address
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mæstare, mæster from Middle Low German meister, mēster, from Old Saxon mēstar, from Old French maistre, from Latin magister. Doublet of mästare and magister.

parole.significato: a meal (occasion of eating (a more substantial amount of) food)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German maltit.

From Old Swedish mångel, from Middle Low German mangelen, from Old Saxon mangalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *mangalōn, from Latin mangō (“dealer, monger”). Attested since 1527. Cognate with Old Norse manga, Old English mangian, Middle High German mangâri.
From Old Swedish moste, from Middle Low German moste, past tense of môten, from Old Saxon motan.
From Old Swedish mat, from Middle Low German mât (modern Low German mâte, mât); ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *metan (“to measure”). Compare måtta.
From Old Swedish mata f, mate m, from Middle Low German māte, from Old Saxon metan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *metaną.

parole.significato: to direct, to aim (often of a punch or other aggressive act)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mata, from Middle Low German māten, from Old Saxon metan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *metaną.

From Old Swedish mylna, mölna, mölla, from Middle Low German molne, molle (cf. German Mühle, Danish mølle, Icelandic mylna). From Late Latin molina, derivation of earlier mola (“mill”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Inherited from Old Swedish menia, mynia, from Middle Low German minie, from Latin minium.

parole.significato: pattern; that from which a copy is made
parole.testo: From Middle Low German munster, from Old French monstre‚ from Latin monstrare.
From Old Swedish nalkas, nalka, from Middle Low German naleken.
Attested in Swedish at least since 1528; from Middle Low German narre, from Old Saxon *narro, from Proto-West Germanic *narrō. Cognate with Danish nar and Norwegian Nynorsk narr.
From Middle Low German nēderdêl, equivalent to neder (“down[wards]”) + del (“part, section”). Compare Middle High German niderteil (obsolete German Niederteil).
Borrowed from Middle Low German nēgede, from Old Saxon *nāhitha, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwiþu.
From Middle Low German nicken, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *hnīgan (“to bow”). Equivalent to nick + -a.
Borrowed from Middle Low German nok, nokke. Cognate of Dutch nok. Likely cognate of Icelandic hnokki. Compare origin of nocka, nucka.

parole.significato: careful; about someone who takes great care to make things properly
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nōgha, from Middle Low German nouwe (“narrow”). Compare German genau.
nog + -sam, from Middle Low German nochsam (“sufficient”). Originally in the sense "sufficient", shift in sense influenced by noga, noggrann.
From Middle Low German nachtegale, from Old Saxon nahtagala.
From Old Swedish næra, from Middle Low German neren, from Old Saxon nerian.

parole.significato: nourishment, food; that which nurtures or nourishes an organism; the lunch on your table
parole.testo: From Old Swedish næring, from Middle Low German neringe, from neren + -inge, equivalent to nära + -ing.

parole.significato: nose of a human or other primate (or anthropomorphized being, especially if having a human-like nose, but sometimes mor…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish næsa, older form *nas, pl. nasar, influenced by Middle Low German nese (cf. Norwegian Bokmål nese, Danish næse), from Old Norse nǫs (pl. nasar, nasir), from Proto-Germanic *nasō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Doublet of nos.
Borrowed from Middle Low German nesewīs or German naseweis. Originally about dogs with a keen sense of smell. By surface analysis, näsa + vis. Compare Danish næsvis.

parole.significato: absolute necessity, the bare essentials of life
parole.testo: Superficially equivalent to nöd + torft, from Old Swedish nødhthorft. Arguably borrowed from Middle Low German nōtorft, nōttroft, from Old Saxon nōdthurft, from nōd (“need”) + thurft (“need”). Related to Old Norse þurft, which is from Proto-Germanic *þurftiz. Cognate of Danish nødtørft, German Notdu
Calque of Middle Low German unaflatlik, equivalent to o- + av- + låta + -lig. Compare German unablässig.

o- + förblommerad, the latter compound the past participle of rare förblommera, from Middle Low German vorblômen, vorblûmen, meaning "garnish with flowers". Compare Danish uforblommet, German unverblümt, English unflourished.
From Old Swedish oforrætter, from Middle Low German unvorrechten, unvorrechtinge.
Borrowed from Middle Low German unvorwītlik. Doublet of tillvita and vite.
Borrowed from Middle Low German unvorwegen. First attested in 1541.

From Old Swedish ohyra (“monster; pest”), from Middle Low German unhuren, ungehuren, related to German Ungeheuer (“monster”). When used to describe pests, arguably of a Nordic origin. Compare Old Norse hýrr (“pleasant; mild”), together with prefix o- (“un-”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German olie, from Latin oleum.

Old Swedish ursak, a compound of ur- and sak (“legal dispute”), in other words "origin of the legal matter". Borrowed from Middle Low German orsake. Compare Danish årsag, Norwegian årsak, Dutch oorzaak, and German Ursache.

From Middle Low German orsaken, equivalent of orsak (“a cause”) + -a. Cognate with Danish årsage, Norwegian Bokmål forårsake, Norwegian Nynorsk forårsake, forårsaka, Middle Dutch orsaken, older Dutch oorzaken and older German ursachen.

parole.significato: locality, place, location; a group of houses (of any size: hamlet, village, town, city...)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ort, from Old Saxon ord, from Proto-West Germanic *oʀd, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“sharp point, place”). Cognate with Middle English ord, North Frisian od (“tip, place, beginning”), Dutch oord (“place, region”), German Ort (“location, place, position”), Danish od (“a point”)
From Old Swedish orætfærdhogher, from Middle Low German unrechtverdich, equivalent to o- + rättfärdig.
Inherited from Old Swedish ostyrogher, from Middle Low German unstürich. By surface analysis, o- + styra + -ig.

parole.significato: sexual immorality, fornication (sexual intercourse considered illicit)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German untucht, equivalent to o- (“un-”) + tukt (“discipline”). Compare German Unzucht.

parole.significato: a bag; an unpleasant older woman
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pack, packe, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly from a group of words related to Proto-Germanic *pakkô (“pack”).
Inherited from Old Swedish pakke, from Middle Low German packe, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-West Germanic *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

parole.significato: jacket, formal (or formal casual) piece of clothing worn on the upper body outside a shirt or blouse

parole.testo: From Middle Low German palsternake, pasternake, from Latin pastināca.

parole.significato: panel (most senses, e.g. a wall panel, a panel of experts)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German panele (“wall covering”), and English panel (other senses).
From Old Swedish panzar, borrowed from Middle Low German pantzer, from Italian panciera, from Latin pantex.

parole.significato: pledge, pawn, item deposited at a pawnshop or otherwise given as a security
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish panter (“deposit”). From Middle Low German pant and Old Norse pantr. First attested in the early half of the 14th century.
Borrowed from Middle Low German persik, ultimately from Latin persicum.
Inherited from Old Swedish päkilhuva, from Middle Low German pekelhūwe. Later influenced by German Pickelhaube.
Probably borrowed from Middle Low German pipe. Doublet of pipa. Of tube spouts and open spouts by extension.
Probably via Middle Low German pissen from Old French pissier (“to piss”)
Probably borrowed from Middle Low German pissen, from Old French pissier (“to piss”), all imitative. Attested in Swedish since 16th century.
Borrowed from Middle Low German pladeren, pladderen. Likely originally onomatopoeic, compare origin of Latin blaterāre, German plaudern, plappern, Ancient Greek φλέδων (phlédōn).
From Middle Low German planke, from Latin planca.

parole.significato: a plank, a board (sawn piece of timber, not too thin – compare bräda)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German planke, from Latin planca.
Derived from Middle Low German plicht, from Old Saxon *pliht, from Proto-West Germanic *plihti.

parole.significato: a plug (piece of wood, metal, or other substance used to stop or fill a hole)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish plugger, from Middle Low German plock, pluck. From Middle Low German plunderen. Probably from the noun Plunder (“stuff”). Possibly originally in the sense "to remove household utensils by coercion". Further origin beyond German is unclear. Cognate of German plündern, English plunder, Dutch plunderen, Danish plyndre.

parole.significato: to have a habit to do, to tend to do something
parole.testo: From Old Swedish plægha, from Middle Low German plegen, from Old Saxon plegan, from Proto-West Germanic *plehan.

parole.significato: a pain, a plague, a torment
parole.testo: From Old Swedish plagha, from Middle Low German plage, from Latin plaga (“plague, injury, wound”).
From Old Swedish plān, from Middle Low German plân, from Latin planum. Doublet of plan.
From Middle Low German plate, from Vulgar Latin *platta, *plattus.

parole.significato: sudden (happening quickly and with little or no warning)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German plutzlik or German plötzlich.

parole.significato: to insistently demand or lay claim to (something, sometimes something abstract)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German puchen (“bang, hit”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German poppele, from Latin populus (“poplar”).

parole.significato: potty: small, usually plastic, chamber pot used as toilet for small children
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German pot, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”). Doublet of pott.

parole.significato: to foist upon, to push (trick or force someone to accept something (undesirable))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German prachen (“to beg, to panhandle”). Compare dialectal German prachern and Pracher, as well as Saterland Frisian prakken (“to press, to push”).

From Middle Low German pracht, from Old High German braht (“crackling noise”), from Proto-Germanic *brahtaz (“cracking, snapping”), referring to the sound of applause. Influenced by German prangen (“to show off”).
From Middle Low German praten, probably of imitative origin, though note also Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“boastful talk”). Compare English prate and prattle, Faroese práta.
From Middle Low German pricken, from Old Saxon *prikkian, from the verb Proto-Germanic *prikjaną (“to prick”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German prente, from Old French priente, preinte, from Old French preindre, priembre, from Latin premere.

parole.significato: a narrow, dark, passage between e.g. two buildings; a very narrow street
parole.testo: From Old Swedish prang, borrowed from Middle Low German prangen, from Old Saxon *prangan, from Proto-West Germanic *prangan (“to press”).

parole.significato: to test, to try (subject to a test)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish prøva, from Middle Low German prôven, from Late Latin probō (“test, try, examine, approve, show to be good or fit, prove”, verb), from probus (“good, worthy, excellent”), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-bhwo- (“being in front, prominent”), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-, *per- (“towar
From Middle Low German puke.
From Middle Low German pumpe (“ship's pump”), of imitative origin and often connected to Spanish bomba (“pump”).
From archaic pärsa, from Middle Low German perse. Cognate of Danish perse, Dutch pers. Doublet of press.

parole.significato: a (stout) stick used as a weapon; a cudgel, a club
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German pōk. Cognate with Dutch pook and English poke.
From Old Swedish rama, borrowed from Middle Low German rāme, from Old Saxon hrama.

parole.significato: a vine, a bine, a long climbing shoot of a plant
parole.testo: Ultimately from Middle Low German [Term?], related to Proto-West Germanic *wrankijan, Norwegian Nynorsk ranke, German Ranke and Dutch rank

parole.significato: a partridge (any bird of the genera Perdix or Alectoris)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish raphōns, from Middle Low German raphōn (“partridge”), possibly from Proto-Slavic *arębъ (“partridge”). Compare origin of German Rebhuhn.

parole.significato: partridge (any bird of the genera Perdix or Alectoris, in particular Perdix perdix)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish raphōns, from Middle Low German raphōn (“partridge”).

parole.significato: sweet (agreeable in a tender, charming way)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rar, ultimately borrowed from Latin rarus. False friend of Norwegian rar, Danish rar and English rare, although being etymologically related to all of them.
From Middle Low German rat (“wheel”), from Old Saxon rath.
From Old Swedish redho, redha, from Middle Low German rede; see the related reda for more.
reda (“order”) + -ig. Likely influenced, at least partly, by Middle Low German rēdich.
From Old Swedish redheliker (“due; right; honest”), from Middle Low German redelik. Compare German redlich.

parole.significato: very drunk, perhaps to the point of not being able to take care of oneself
parole.testo: By surface analysis, reda (“take care of (oneself), order”) + -lös (“-less”). Likely from Middle Low German redelōs. If so, the first syllable is closer in meaning to rädda (“rescue”), thus originally "helpless". Compare origin of Dutch reddeloos, German rettlos, Icelandic reiðalauss.

parole.significato: ready; prepared to face whatever is coming one's way
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rēþo, probably from Middle Low German rēde, reide. Cognate with Danish rede, Icelandic reiður.

parole.significato: A bar used to lock or bolt a door
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German regel, further origin disputed. Compare German Riegel, Dutch richel.

parole.significato: considerable in extent (of size, power, etc.); hefty, big, strong, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German reejel, from French réel, whence also reell. Doublet of real and realistisk.

parole.significato: an instance of traveling, "a travel"; a trip, a journey, a voyage, (in the plural) travels, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German reisen, from Old Saxon *reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.
Borrowed from Middle Low German reisenēre.

parole.significato: a long, thin (often flexible) piece used in some construction, for example a lath
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German ribbe, from Proto-Germanic *ribją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ-. Doublet of revben. Cognate of German Rippe, English rib.

Inherited from Old Swedish riddarliker, ridderligh, from Middle Low German ridderlik, from rider (“knight”, literally “rider”) + -līk (from Old Saxon -līk, from Proto-West Germanic *-līk). Analyzable as ryttare + -lig. Cognate of Dutch ridderlijk, German ritterlich.
From Middle Low German richtich or German richtig. Compare Danish rigtig.

From Old Swedish ringa, from Middle Low German ringe, from Old Saxon (gi)ringi (“light”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *reng-ja, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrengʷʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”) and cognate with Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, wring”), Ancient Greek ῥίμ
From Old Swedish ringebloma, an alternation of earlier ringelbloma, a borrowing of Middle Low German ringelblome. (Compare German Ringelblume.) By surface analysis, ring + blomma.
From Old Swedish rokker, from Middle Low German rock, from Old Saxon rok, from Proto-West Germanic *(h)rokk, from Proto-Germanic *rukkaz.
Borrowed from Middle Low German roder, from Old Saxon *rōthar, from Proto-West Germanic *rōþr.

parole.significato: a rose (flower, shrub, or heraldic charge)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ros‚ from Middle Low German rose, from Latin rosa.

parole.significato: rosary (prayer beads associated with a set of Marian prayers)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rosenkranz, from Middle Low German or German Rosenkranz, equivalent to ros (“rose”) + krans (“wreath”).
From Middle Low German rōf, from Old Saxon *rōf, from Proto-West Germanic *raub.

parole.significato: a vegetable cultigen with a meaty root from the Rapifera group within the Brassica rapa species, such as the turnip (Br…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rova, probably from Middle Low German rove, a European wanderword related to Latin rapa, rapum (“turnip”) and Greek ῥάφη (rháphē, “turnip”). Doublet of rabba.
Inherited from Old Swedish rugelse, from Middle Low German rūwenisse. Cognate of Old Saxon hreuwan, Old English hrēowan, German reuen, English rue.
From Middle Low German rolle, from Old French rolle (French rôle). Cognate with Danish rulle.
From Middle Low German runt, from Old French reont, similar to Danish rund.
Borrowed from Middle Low German rundēl, from French rondelle, from ronde. Cognate of Danish runddel, German Rundell. Doublet of rond and rondell.

parole.significato: square, tile, box (as on a checkerboard)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rūte, from Old High German rūta, probably from Latin rūta (“rue”). Cognates include Danish rude, Norwegian Bokmål rute and German Raute (“rhomb”).
From Middle Low German ruchte, geruchte, derived from the verb rōpen (“to call”), from Old Saxon hrōpan.

parole.significato: to save (prevent from dying or going under more broadly, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rædda, from Middle Low German redden, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną. Cognate with Danish redde. First attested in the early 14th century.
Inherited from Old Swedish rännesten, equivalent to ränna + sten. Likely borrowed from Middle Low German renstēn, rennenstēn. Cognate of Danish rendesten. Compare also German Rinnstein.

From Old Swedish rætganger, rættarganger, from Middle Low German rechtgank, equivalent to rätt + -e- + gång. Cognate with Danish rettergang, Norwegian Bokmål rettergang, Norwegian Nynorsk rettargang, German Rechtsgang and Dutch rechtsgang.

parole.significato: righteousness, the quality of being righteous (rättfärdig)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rætfærdhoghet, from Middle Low German rechtverdicheit, equivalent to rättfärdig + -het. Compare German rechtfertigkeit, Danish retfærdighed.

parole.significato: a right (something one is legally entitled to)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rechticheit.
Borrowed from Middle Low German redik, from Old Saxon *rādik, from Proto-West Germanic *rādik, borrowed from Latin rādīcem. Doublet of radikal, rot, and rädisa.
Borrowed from Middle Low German rādebrāken, from rāt (“wheel”) + brāken (“break”). Cognate of Danish radbrække, German radebrechen, Dutch radbraken.

parole.significato: to happen to do, to accidentally do; do without purpose or intention
parole.testo: Derived from Old Swedish raka, borrowed from Middle Low German rāken (“to touch, hit”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *rakōn (“to choose a direction”).

parole.significato: rat; an omnivorous rodent of the genus Rattus.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rotta, from Middle Low German rotte, from Proto-Germanic *rattō.
From Old Swedish rölika, from Middle Low German roleke, rolik, diminutive of *role (“roll; rolled shape”) (referring to the shape of the leaves).
From Middle Low German sä̂lich, older form of sêlich, from Old Saxon sālig, from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg.
Borrowed from Middle Low German samentkumst or German Zusammenkunft. Cognate of Dutch samenkomst, Danish sammenkomst. Related to komma + samman.
Inherited from Old Swedish samet, from Middle Low German sammet, from Ancient Greek ἑξάμιτον (hexámiton). Cognate of English samite, German Samt, Sammet.

parole.significato: and, and also, plus, as well as
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sament, samt (“together with”)

parole.significato: sunk (the state (of a ship or the like) of no longer being able to float due to damage)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sank, from Middle Low German in sank.
From Middle Low German schavot, German Schafott, from Old French chafaut. Cognate of Italian catafalco and French échafaud. Doublet of katafalk.

From Old Swedish seghiare, seghare, säyare, from Middle Low German seyger, sēer, seyer, segger (“scale, balance, tower clock”), probably from Middle High German seigære (“scale, clock”). parole.significato: visibility (ability to see long distances, contingent on fogginess, obstacles, etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sicht, from Proto-Germanic *sihti. See German Sicht for more.
From Old Swedish sikte, from Middle Low German sichte. Compare sikt.
From Old Swedish simpel, from Middle Low German simpel, from Latin simplex.

parole.significato: roll of the dice resulting in five and two
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sinke (“five”) and dus (“two”).
From Old Swedish sinne, sin, from Middle Low German sin, from Old Saxon *sinn, from Proto-West Germanic *sinn.

parole.significato: pertaining to the senses, capable of being perceived by the senses
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sinnelīk, sinlīk, or German sinnlich. Equivalent to sinne + -lig. Compare Danish sindelig.
Borrowed from Middle Low German sinnerīke or German sinnreich, equivalent to sinne + rik. Cognate of Danish sindrig.

parole.significato: a name given to certain finches of the genera Carduelis, Acanthis, and Spinus.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish siseka, from Middle Low German sīsek, sīseke(n), apparently ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čižь.
From Middle Low German schafferīe, cognate of German Schafferei, equivalent to skaffa + -eri. Compare dated skaffare (“supplier”).
Inherited from Old Swedish skalker, from Middle Low German scalc, schalk. Cognate of German Schalk. Doublet of marskalk.

parole.significato: A sconce; a type of small fort or other fortification.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish skanz. Borrowed from Middle Low German schanse, schanze. First attested in 1506. Cognate with Danish skanse, Norwegian skanse, and English sconce.

parole.significato: an executioner, a headsman (executioner that beheads)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German scharprichter, equivalent to skarp + rättare. Compare avrätta and Danish skarpretter.

parole.significato: to happen; in particular what happens during some extended period of time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ske, from Middle Low German schên, from Old Saxon skehan, from Proto-West Germanic *skehan. Cognate with Danish ske, Norwegian skje, German geschehen, Dutch geschieden, Limburgish sji-jje.

parole.significato: a rail (metal bar forming part of the track for a railroad)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skena, from Middle Low German schene, from Old Saxon scina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu, from Proto-Germanic *skinō. Influenced by German Schiene. First attested in 1478.
From Old Swedish skinbar (“brilliant; shining”), from Middle Low German schīnbār. Cognate of German scheinbar. Superficially equivalent to sken + -bar.
Inherited from Old Swedish skik, from Middle Low German schik (“form; order”). Likely cognate of French chic.
From Old Swedish skikka, from Middle Low German schicken "to send" (German schicken, Dutch schikken). Cognate with Swedish ske "to happen, to occur". Compare Trøndelag Norwegian sjekk (“to send”).

parole.significato: to depict, to portray, to describe
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German schilderen. Cognate of Dutch schilderen, German schildern. Doublet of skylt and sköld.
Calque of Middle Low German schomaker, equivalent to sko (“shoe”) + -makare (“-maker”).
Inherited from Old Swedish skona, from Middle Low German schonen, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunōn.
From Old Swedish skōpa, borrowing from Middle Low German schōpe, from Proto-Germanic *skōpō.
Likely from Middle Low German schral or Dutch schraal. Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål skral. Possibly related with skrå (“guild”).

parole.significato: a rail, a bar, a fence, a screen, a desk; making two sections of a room (in a church, court of law, or pub)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schrank, cognate with German Schrank, used in Swedish since 1561.
From Middle Low German schranke (“barrier; bar”). Cognate of German Schranke (“barrier; limit”).

parole.significato: shot (small metal balls used as ammunition)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schrôt, from Old Saxon skrōt. Compare German Schrot and German Schrott, Dutch schroot.
Borrowed from Middle Low German schruve. Compare to and Danish skrue and Norwegian Nynorsk skruve (older spelling of skrue).

parole.significato: to boast, to brag; to talk loudly in praise of oneself
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schruten (“to puff, snort”), probably an expressive/imitative development of Old Saxon hrutan (“to snore, make a noise”).
Derived from Middle Low German schrēdere, schrādere, schrȫder; see German schroten (“to grind, chip”) for more. Insect name from making scissor-like motions with the middle legs. Doublet of skräda.
Likely borrowed from Middle Low German schūven.

parole.significato: to take shelter from the rain
parole.testo: Cognate to older Danish skule (“hide, take shelter”). Probably a loan from Middle Low German schulen (“to hide”), compare Dutch schuilen (“to take shelter”).
From Old Swedish skyldenær, from Middle Low German schuldenēr. Compare Norwegian skyldner, Dutch schuldenaar, German Schuldner.

parole.significato: to avoid (due to fear, disgust, or the like), to shun
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schǖwen, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhijan. Compare origin of skygg.
Clipping of beskydda, inherited from Old Swedish beskydda, borrowed from Middle Low German beschudden. Attested since 1640.

parole.significato: a shovel (for moving material (with a more concave profile and often upturned edges) – compare spade)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German schüffel, schüffele, schuffele, schūfele, schūfle.

parole.significato: a sign (clearly visible, generally flat object bearing a short message in words or pictures)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schilt, same word as sköld. Similar to Danish and Norwegian skilt n
Inherited from Old Swedish skäkta, from Middle Low German schecht, from schacht (“shaft”). Doublet of schakt and skaft.
From Old Swedish skiælmber, from Middle Low German schelm. Disputed origin. Cognate of German Schelm, Dutch schelm, Danish skælm, Icelandic skelmir.

parole.significato: desecrate, defile, violate (treat (something ordinarily respected) with grave disrespect)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skænda, from Middle Low German schenden, from Old Saxon *skendian, from Proto-West Germanic *skandijan. Cognate of Danish skænde, Dutch schenden, German schänden, Old English scendan.
From Old Swedish skændeliker, from Middle Low German schendelīk (equivalent to German schändlich), from German Schande (“disgrace”). Equivalent to skända + -lig.
From Old Swedish skænkia, from Middle Low German schenken, from Old Saxon skenkian, from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną.
From Middle Low German scherm, from Old Saxon *skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi (“fur, pelt, covering, screen”).

parole.significato: a skirmish (a brief battle between small groups)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schermützel, from Italian scaramuccia. Cognate of English skirmish, German Scharmützel, and Dutch schermutseling.

parole.significato: a cabinet, a cupboard, a locker (either separate from, or built into, a wall, usually with shelves)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skap, from Middle Low German schap, from Old Saxon skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą. Cognate with Icelandic skápur.

From Old Swedish skön, from Middle Low German schö̂ne, from Old Saxon skōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz (“beautiful, shining”), related to *skuþōną, which yielded skåda (“to watch, to behold”). Compare German schön, English sheen, Danish skøn.
From Middle Low German slachten, though Swedish had its own cognate word for "slaughter", a descendant of Old Norse slátra.
Borrowed from Middle Low German slam. Cognate of German Schlamm. Further origin disputed. Attested since 1587.
From Old Swedish slember, from Middle Low German slim, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz. Related to German schlimm (“bad”).
From Middle Low German slicken, from Proto-Germanic *slikkōną.

parole.significato: snake, slither, wind (move in a winding manner)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slingeren, from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną.

parole.significato: a slut, a floozy, a trollop (promiscuous woman)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish slinka, from Middle Low German slinken, from Old Saxon *slinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *slinkan, from Proto-Germanic *slinkaną. The noun is derived from the verb.
From Middle Low German slipen, from Proto-West Germanic *slīpan (“to grind, whet, sharpen”).

parole.significato: to slip, to slide, to skid (due to lack of traction, for example during slippery road conditions)
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Middle Low German slīren, at least as a naval term. Compare origin of English slide, slither, Middle English slideren.

parole.significato: a castle, a palace (large, grand building serving or previously serving as a residence for royalty or nobility (where f…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slot, from Proto-Germanic *slutą (see Proto-West Germanic *slot for more).

Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, probably from a Proto-Germanic *slūhaz (“sneaking, creeping”), perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leuǵ (“to crawl, slide”), if the original sense referred to sneaking and sliding. Cognate of German schlau, Dutch sluw, Norwegian slu.
Borrowed from Middle Low German slump.

parole.significato: to doze, to snooze, to slumber
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German slummern or German schlummern.

parole.significato: over, finished; which has come to an end
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slūt.
Borrowed from Middle Low German slūne (“promiscuous woman”). Cognate with English slut.

parole.significato: an ill-mannered boy or young man; a punk, a brat
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German slungel. Cognate of German Schlingel (obsolete form Schlüngel). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną. Compare origin of slunga and slänga.
From Old Swedish slækt, borrowed from Middle Low German slecht (“family, lineage”), from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, from the verb *slahaną.

parole.significato: an interrelated group (in some sense – intuitively biologically related, with sense extensions similar to "breed," etc.…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slechte.

parole.significato: to drag (with difficulty) over a surface
parole.testo: From Old Swedish slēpa, from Middle Low German slēpen, from Old Saxon *slēpian, from Proto-West Germanic *slaipijan.
From Middle Low German slösen (“to lounge, loaf about”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk sløsa.
Likely borrowed from Middle Low German smacken. Cognate of Dutch smakken. Likely originally onomatopoeic. See also smäcka, smaska, smocka.
Inherited from Old Swedish smaker, from Middle Low German smak, smake, from Old Saxon *smakk, *smak, from Proto-West Germanic *smakku.

parole.significato: to taste (sample the flavor of something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish smaka, from Middle Low German smaken, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *smakōn, equivalent to smak + -a. Cognate with Danish smage, Middle English smaken.

parole.significato: to stroke softly and tenderly; to caress, to stroke, to rub, to fondle, to pet, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish smēkia, from Middle Low German smêken. Cognate with German schmeicheln. Doublet of smickra.

parole.significato: a batter; a thin, mostly liquid mixture of flour, some liquid (such as water or milk), and possibly other ingredients,…
parole.testo: Origin uncertain. Probably from Middle Low German smette, smitte (“mush or paste used by the linen weavers to strengthen the hoist", also "stain, mark, blemish”). Compare Saterland Frisian Smitte (“a kind of paste or glue used to strengthen the lift and shear in weaving”). If so, cognate also with E

parole.significato: flexible and in good control of one's body
parole.testo: From Old Swedish smidogher, from Middle Low German smīdich. Equivalent to smida + -ig, in the sense "forgeable". Compare German geschmeidig.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smitte (“stain”), derived from the verb smitte, from Old Saxon smītan (“to smite”, originally "to smear, coat").
Borrowed from Middle Low German smecker, from Proto-Germanic *smikraz. Cognate of Old English smicer.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smēden, smāden, from Proto-Germanic *smēhijaną (“belittle”). Compare origin of försmå, Dutch smaad and German schmähen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smechten, smachten, from Proto-Germanic *smēhaz. Cognate of German schmachten, Dutch smachten, Danish smægte.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smerte, ultimately from the source of Etymology 3 below.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smerten, from Old Saxon *smertan, from Proto-West Germanic *smertan.
Borrowed from Middle Low German snacken (“to speak, talk”). Compare Danish snakke, Norwegian Bokmål snakke and Norwegian Nynorsk snakka.

parole.significato: to snatch, to snap (take with a short, quick motion, literally or figuratively)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German snappen (“speak rapidly”), which is probably related to snavel (“beak, snout”), from Old Saxon *snavel, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz. Cognate of German schnappen, Dutch snappen. Compare origin of snopen.

parole.significato: to snore; to make noises while asleep
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German snorken, snarken, from Old Saxon *snarkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *snarkōn.
Possibly from Middle Low German snaven. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk snåva, Middle English snaperen.

Inherited from Old Swedish snitkare, snidhkare, from Middle Low German sniddeker, snidker, snicker. Cognate of Danish snedker and Norwegian Bokmål snekker. By surface analysis, snicka + -are. The dialectal verb snicka is from Old Swedish snikka, from Old Norse *sníðka, from sníða (from whence also s
Derived from Middle Low German snellen (“hurry”).

First attested in the compound afsnit (“section”) by Gustavus Adolphus in 1621, from Old Swedish snīdh, snēdh, but effected by Middle Low German snit (German Schnitt; cf. schnitzen, Swedish snitsa), from Old Norse sníð, from Proto-Germanic *snīþaną. Related to snida (“to carve”). Doublet of sned and
Originally meaning "snout," from Middle Low German snûte, from Old Saxon *snūt, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt.

parole.significato: a bird in the Scolopacidae family
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German sneppe, after the long, thin beak of the bird, from or related to Old Saxon *snabul, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz (“snout, beak, mouth”). Cognate of German Schnepfe, Dutch snip, Faroese mýrisnípa. First attested in 1664.

parole.significato: sugar; sucrose in the form of small crystals
parole.testo: From Old Swedish soker, from Middle Low German sucker, from Italian zucchero, from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), from Persian شکر (šakar).
From Old Swedish sumliker, somliker, probably from Middle Low German somelīk, somlīk, sumlīk, from Old Saxon sum + *-līk. Cognate with Old High German sumalīh and Dutch sommige.
Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Cognate of German sorgfältig.

parole.significato: to select some parts (to be kept or the like) and reject other parts; to sift, to sort, to winnow, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German süvern, sovern, suvern (“to clean”) or a related form, cognate with German säubern.

parole.significato: a lever used to control some machine; a lever, a rod, a handle, a stick, a joystick, a control
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spaker (“rod, stick, lever”), from Middle Low German spake, cognate with Danish spag (“spoke”), Dutch spaak (“spoke”), and English spoke.
Inherited from Old Swedish spe, from Middle Low German spē. Doublet of spy.

From Old Swedish speia, from Middle Low German spējen, from Old Saxon *spehōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną. Cognate of Danish speide, German spähen. Doublet of spå. See also origin for spion.
Borrowed from Middle Low German spēære, spēer, spēger, equivalent to speja + -are. Cognate with Danish spejder, German Späher.

parole.significato: a play, a game; a person's or animal's happy, joyous movement or entertainment; activity for amusement only; a pursuit…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spil, from Middle Low German spil and Old Saxon spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil.

Old Swedish spill, from Middle Low German spille, from Old Saxon spinnila, from Proto-West Germanic *spinnilu, cognate with German Spindel and English spindle. With time, the Swedish word has adopted the declension pattern of spel in Etymology 1. Note that spindel is also a Swedish word.
Derivation of spett (“spit, skewer”), from Old Swedish spet, probably a borrowing from Middle Low German lance, spear.
Borrowed from Middle Low German spitze, from Proto-Germanic *spitjaz. Compare German Spitze.
From Old Swedish split, borrowed from Middle Low German spliten (“to split”). First attested in 1533.

parole.significato: slat, tongue (part of a board or plank which fits into a groove)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German spunt, ultimately from Latin expūnctum.

parole.significato: to distribute, to spread, to disseminate
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spridha, probably the same word as spredha, from Middle Low German sprēden, spreiden, from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną (“to spread”). Cognate with English spread and German spreiten. Due to the absence of this word in Old Icelandic, the Swedish word as well as Danish sprede, Norwegi
From Old Swedish sprāk, borrowed from Middle Low German sprāke, from Old Saxon sprāka. Displaced native tunga, mål in this sense.
Borrowed from Middle Low German or German Staket, from Old French estachette, from Italian staccetta. Doublet of stake.
Borrowed from Middle Low German stappelen.
From Middle Low German stat, from Latin status.
Inherited from Old Swedish stenkol (equivalent to sten + kol), from Middle Low German stēnkolen, stēnkolene.

parole.significato: a small, thin (metal) object (often used to fasten or connect something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German stift, steft, a variant of stippen (“to nick”). Cognate of German Stift.

parole.significato: a diocese, a bishopric, a see (region administered by a bishop, especially in Sweden)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German sticht, stift. Cognate of German Stift. More details at stifta.
Inherited from Old Swedish stikta, from Middle Low German stichten, from Proto-West Germanic *stiftijan conflated with *stihtijan.
From Middle Low German stille, from Old Saxon stilli, from Proto-West Germanic *stillī.

parole.significato: to stink, to reek (smell very bad)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stinka, from Middle Low German stinken, from Old Saxon stinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *stinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną. First attested in 1491. Cognate with Dutch and German stinken, Danish stinke, English stink.
From Middle Low German stȫven, from Old Saxon *stiovan, from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan.

From Middle Low German straffen, from Proto-West Germanic *strēpōn, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to *streupan (“to squeeze, press, graze”). Compare with German Strafe. Etymologies 2, 3, and 4 below are all clippings of compounds from Etymology 1.

parole.significato: a short(ish) line; a line, a dash
parole.testo: Used in this form in the Bible translation of 1541. From Middle Low German streke, from Old Saxon *striki, from Proto-West Germanic *striki. Cognate with Norwegian strek, Danish streg, corresponding to Gothic striks, Middle Low German streke, Middle High German and German Strich, related to German v
From Middle Low German strunt, from Old Saxon *strunt, from Proto-West Germanic *strunt.
Inherited from Old Swedish strudz, probably borrowed from Middle Low German strūs, strūse, strūts, strūtse, ultimately from Late Latin strūthiō, from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn).
From Old Swedish strækkia, from Middle Low German strecken, from Old Saxon *strekkian.

parole.significato: rough, coarse, harsh, raspy (not smooth to the touch, of a surface, or figuratively)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German stref, and ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *strībaną (“to be stiff”).

parole.significato: a ray, a beam (of light, radiation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German strâle, from Old Saxon strāla, from Proto-West Germanic *strālu (“beam”), also "arrow."

parole.significato: to sprain (injure a body part through wrenching)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German stūken. Cognate of German stauchen. Compare origin of stock, stöka.
Borrowed from Middle Low German stursch. Cognate of German stur, störrisch, Dutch stuurs.

parole.significato: stiff; unbending, which does not easily fold
parole.testo: Used in Old Swedish. Cognate with Old Danish and Middle Low German stif, related to Latin stipes (pole, beam). The second meaning (skilled) used since 1614. From Middle Low German stīf, from Old Saxon *stīf, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steyp.
Derived from Middle Low German stüver, cognate with Dutch stuiver, Danish styver, English stiver. First attested in 1546.

parole.significato: a place, a location, a position
parole.testo: From Middle Low German stellen, from Old Saxon stellian. Cf German Stelle.

parole.significato: a voice (language; words; speech; expression; signification of feeling or opinion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German stemmen, from Old Saxon *stemnian, from Proto-West Germanic *stabnijan, from Proto-Germanic *stabnijaną.

Formed from the verb stå (“to stand, be upright”), likely with influence from Middle Low German stān, from Old Saxon stān. Cognate with English stand, Danish stand, Norwegian Bokmål stand, Norwegian Nynorsk stand.

From a verb meaning "to move things around," from or cognate Middle Low German stûken (“to push, bump, compress”), from Old Saxon *stūkan, from Proto-Germanic *stūkaną (“to be stiff, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to pound, push, beat”). By surface analysis, stök + -a. Possibly related

parole.significato: to descend or fall or (with a particle like samman (“together”)) collapse uncontrollably
parole.testo: From Old Swedish styrta, from Middle Low German störten.
Borrowed from Middle Low German stȫver. Cognate of Danish støver, German Stöber.
Inherited from Old Swedish sunder, from Middle Low German sunt, from Old Saxon *sund, from Proto-West Germanic *sund.

Arguably from Middle Low German sūrmūlen. Arguably past participle of verb surmula. In folk etymology interpreted as sur (“sour”) + mulen (“cloudy; overcast”), for example in the 1749 dictionary by Olof Lind. Compare Danish surmule. See also Dutch zuurmuil, archaic German Sauermaul, English sourpuss

parole.significato: weak; lacking in force or ability
parole.testo: From Middle Low German swak, from Old Saxon *swak, from Proto-West Germanic *swak. Compare with German schwach. The form with -g- is due to Danish influence.

From Old Swedish svavel, from Middle Low German swavel, swevel, from Old Saxon sweval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz. Cognate of German Schwefel, Dutch zwavel, Danish svovl, Old English swefl, Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌹𐌱𐌻𐍃 (swibls).

parole.significato: to bend (or compress, etc.) sharply and then regain shape (of for example a springboard)
parole.testo: Likely a merger of Old Swedish svigha (“bend”) and Middle Low German swichten (“succumb”). Compare Dutch zwichten (“yield”), Old High German giswiftōn (“quieten down”). Doublet of svika.
From Middle Low German swimen, from Proto-Germanic *swīmaną (“to sway, to swoon”). Cf. Danish and Norwegian Bokmål besvime, Norwegian Nynorsk svima av, English sweem, Dutch zwijm.

parole.significato: to swing (move (something) in an arcing motion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German swingen, from Proto-West Germanic *swingan. Cognate of German schwingen, English swing. Doublet of svänga and schvung.

parole.significato: to cease, to vanish, to disappear, to diminish, to fade
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svinda, svinna, borrowed from Middle Low German swinden, from Old Saxon swindan, from Proto-West Germanic *swindan.

From Middle Low German swulst or German Schwulst, from Middle High German swulst (“tumor, growth”), itself from German schwellen (“to swell”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”). Doublet of svall and svullnad.

parole.significato: a sister-in-law; a sister of someone's spouse
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svæghirska, from Middle Low German swegersche.
Borrowed from Middle Low German swengen, from Proto-West Germanic *swangijan. Cognate of Old English swenġan, Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐍃𐍅𐌰𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (afswaggwjan). Doublet of svinga.

parole.significato: to float (in the air), to hover, to soar
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svæva‚ likely borrowed from Middle Low German swēven, from Old Saxon *swivian, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną. Doublet of sviva.

parole.significato: a brother-in-law; a brother of someone's spouse
parole.testo: * The SAOB dictionary states that this is inherited from Old Swedish svāgher, swoger. * From Middle Low German swāger, from Old Saxon *swāgar, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“husband's father”).
Likely from Middle Low German swārmodich, equivalent svårmod + -ig. Compare Middle Dutch swâermoedich, Middle High German swærmüetic. Cognate of Dutch zwaarmoedig, German schwermütig.
From Old Swedish syl, from Middle Low German sul, sülle, sille.

parole.significato: jam (sweet mixture of fruit boiled with sugar, usually with a fairly loose consistency – compare marmelad)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sulten, from Old Saxon *sultia, from Proto-Germanic *sultijō.
Inherited from Old Swedish sunderliker, from Middle Low German sünderlīk. Cognate of Danish synderlig, German sonderlich, English sunderly.
From Middle Low German seker, from Old Saxon sikur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur, from Latin sēcūrus.
From Old Swedish sikerhet, from Middle Low German sekerheit, akin to säker + -het.

parole.significato: only used in sälla sig till (“to join”)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sælla, a calque of Middle Low German sellen, equivalent to sälle + -a. Compare German gesellen.

From Old Swedish sælle (“a companion”), from Middle Low German selle, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *saljô (“a roommate”). Related to sal (“a large room, a hall”). Cognate with Danish and Norwegian selle.
From Middle Low German seltsam (“rare”), from Proto-Germanic *seldanē. First part is the same root as in sällan and sällsynt. Compare Dutch zeldzaam, Danish sælsom.

From Old Swedish sælskap, sællaskap, a calque of Middle Low German selschap, equivalent to sälle (“companion”) + -skap (“-ship”). Cognate with Danish selskab, Norwegian selskap. Compare German Gesellschaft, Dutch gezelschap.
Inherited from Old Swedish takel, from Middle Low German takel. Cognate of Dutch takel, English tackle.
From Old Swedish talgher, from Middle Low German talch, from Old Saxon *talg, from Proto-West Germanic *talg, from Proto-Germanic *talgaz.

From Old Swedish þanke, borrowed from Middle Low German danke, from Old Saxon thanc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz, with the initial consonant of the related verb Swedish tänka (“think”). The Middle Low German word has also been borrowed to Danish tanke, Norwegian tanke, and Icelandic þanki.
From Old Swedish dapper, from Middle Low German dapper, tapper. Further origin disputed. Possibly cognate with Old Norse dapr (“heavy”), German tapfer (“dauntless”) and English dapper.
Borrowed from Middle Low German tasche. Cognate of German Tasche. Doublet of task and taskspelare.

parole.significato: a tuft or lock of hair
parole.testo: From Old Swedish test, related to tesa (“to pull out wool”), from Middle Low German tēsen, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *taisan (“to pull apart, tug”).

Inherited from Old Swedish til frids, til freds, likely from Middle Low German to-vrede. Literally "at peace". Cognate of German zufrieden. Compare phrases like till dess, till havs, till sjöss, till fots, till bords.

parole.significato: temporary; valid for a brief period of time
parole.testo: Partly from Middle Low German tōvallich, tōvellich from tōval (“occasion, instance”) + -ich and partly from tillfälle + -ig. Cognate with, but with a different meaning than, Danish tilfældig, Norwegian tilfeldig, German zufällig and Dutch toevallig.
From Old Swedish til goþo, a calque of Middle Low German to gōde, equivalent to till + godo. Compare German zugute.

From Old Swedish til saman, til samans, from Middle Low German tosamene. Cognate with Danish tilsammen, Norwegian Bokmål til sammen, tilsammen, as well as the second component of German zusammen, Saterland Frisian tousommen, Middle English tosamen, Dutch tezamen and Luxembourgish zesummen.
