parole.significato: to ascribe, attribute, impute, credit (ascribe characteristics, authorship, ownership, credit, responsibility, as a cau…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German toschriven, equivalent to till + skriva. Cognate of German zuschreiben.

parole.significato: sand lance (fish of the family Ammodytidae)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tobies, from Medieval Latin Tobīās.
Borrowed from Middle Low German trampen, from Old Saxon *trampan, from Proto-West Germanic *trampan (“to step”).
From Middle Low German trappe.

parole.significato: staircase, stairway, stairs, flight of stairs
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trapa, trappa, borrowed from Middle Low German trappe, from Old Saxon *trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā. Similar to Norwegian trapp, Danish trappe and Faroese trappa.
From Middle Low German trechtäre, trechter, from Old Saxon trahtari, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī, from Late Latin tractārius, from Latin trāiectōrium.
Inherited from Old Swedish trava, likely from Middle Low German traven. Cognate of Latin trepidus
Inherited from Old Swedish trinder, from Middle Low German trint (“round”). Doublet of trend.

parole.significato: a (small) disc, a (small) flat cylinder (especially of certain machine and device parts)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German trītze, trīsse. Origin beyond that disputed. Cognate of German triezen, English trice.

parole.significato: a throne (chair of state, also more or less figuratively)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish tron m (compare Old Danish thron), from Middle Low German trōn (corresponding to Middle Dutch troon, Middle High German trōn), from Old French trone, throne (from Latin thronus) and directly from Latin thronus (“throne”), from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “a seat, chair”
Inherited from Old Swedish tros, from Middle Low German trosse, trotze. Cognate of German Trosse, Dutch tros.

From Old Swedish tratz, from Middle Low German trotz, tratz, from Middle High German trotz, trutz, tratz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål tross, Norwegian Nynorsk trass, Danish trods, older forms trotz, tratz, German trotz.
Likely from Middle Low German trotzen. Cognate of Danish trodse, German trotzen.

parole.significato: to walk (in a somewhat slow and dignified manner, usually crossing some boundary); to step, to walk
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trædha, from Middle Low German treden, from Old Saxon *tredan, from Proto-West Germanic *tredan, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną. Doublet of tråda, from Old Norse.

parole.significato: an upper-body garment, excluding outerwear like jackets, especially one worn for warmth and usually not for example a d…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German troye, troie, of uncertain origin, perhaps borrowed from Old French troie (“sweater, cardigan from Troyes”). Cognate with Icelandic treyja and Dutch trui.

parole.significato: to tumble (fall head over heels), to roll
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tummelen, from Proto-Germanic *tūmōną (“to tumble”).

From Old Swedish tvädräkt, from Middle Low German twedracht, nominalization of twedragen (“to disagree”), see tve- (“two-”) + draga (“to pull”), i.e. ”to pull in two directions”. Compare German Zwietracht and Dutch tweedracht.
From Middle Low German twist, from Proto-Germanic *twi-. Compare German Zwist. See also tvedräkt.

From Old Swedish tvifla, borrowed from Middle Low German twīvel (“doubt”), from Old Saxon *twīfal, from Proto-West Germanic *twīfl. Related to Dutch twijfel, German Zweifel and the number two/zwei/två/tve.

parole.significato: tent; a pavilion or portable lodge
parole.testo: From Middle Low German telt, from *Old Saxon *teld, from Proto-West Germanic *teld, from Proto-Germanic *teldą. Displaced Old Swedish tiæld, from Old Norse tjald, from the same Germanic source, compare tjäll.
From Middle Low German temmelîken. Cognate of German ziemlich, Dutch tamelijk, Danish temmelig. By surface analysis, tämlig (“passable”) + -en (adverbial suffix).

parole.significato: a train (locomotive along with a line of coupled railroad cars pulled by it)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German toge, toch, from Old Saxon *tugi, from Proto-West Germanic *tugi. Cognate with Dutch teug, German Zug, Old English tyge. Swedes would make no difference between tåg in vikingatåg (“viking raid”), korståg (“crusade”), fälttåg, krigståg, and plundringståg (“pillage raid”), but i
From Old Swedish untbæra, umbæra, from Middle Low German entbēren, enbēren, equivalent to um- + bära. Cognate of German entbehren, Dutch ontberen.

parole.significato: to pay for, to suffer for
parole.testo: From Old Swedish umgiælda, untgiælda, from Middle Low German untgelden, entgelden, equivalent to um- + gälda. Compare Danish undgælde, German entgelten.
From Old Swedish unt-, from Middle Low German ent-, unt-, um-, from Old Saxon and-. Doublet of an- and ent-.
From Old Swedish undirkasta, calque of Middle Low German underwerpen, equivalent to under- + kasta. Compare German unterwerfen, Dutch onderwerpen.

parole.significato: fail, omit, neglect (to do something (one should do))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German underlaten, equivalent to under + låta. Cognate of German unterlassen. First attested in 1589.

parole.significato: a subject (person ruled over by others, especially others who are not democratically elected, for example a citizen in…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish undirsate, from Middle Low German undersate. Originally in the sense "one who sits below". Cognate with Norwegian undersått.
From Old Swedish untflyia, from Middle Low German entvlen, equivalent to und- + fly. Compare German entfliehen, Old English oþfleon, Gothic 𐌿𐌽𐌸𐌰𐌸𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌷𐌰𐌽 (unþaþliuhan).
From Old Swedish untfa(nga), from Middle Low German untfan(gen), entfan(gen), equivalent to und- + få(nga). Compare Danish undfange, German empfangen, Old English onfon.
From Old Swedish untganga, from Middle Low German untgan, entgan, equivalent to und- + gå. Compare German entgehen.

parole.significato: to manage to escape (from danger or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish untkoma, from Middle Low German entkomen, equivalent to und- + komma. Compare German entkommen.
Inherited from Old Swedish untsætia, from Middle Low German untsetten, entsetten, equivalent to und- + sätta. Compare Danish undsætte, German entsetzen, Dutch ontzetten.
From Old Swedish untvika, from Middle Low German untwiken, entwiken, equivalent to und- + vika. Compare Danish undvige, German entweichen, Norwegian unnvike.
From earlier uppreppa, from Old Swedish upreppa (“to tear open, to bring up again”), from Middle Low German upreppen.
Calque of Middle Low German uprichtich, equivalent to upp + riktig. Compare Danish oprigtig, German aufrichtig.

parole.significato: a rebellion (armed or non-violent resistance to power)
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German uprōr. Cognate of Danish oprør, German Aufruhr, Dutch oproer, Norwegian opprør, English uproar.
Borrowed from Middle Low German upschov. By surface analysis, upp + skov. Cognate of German Aufschub.

parole.significato: defiant towards someone in a position of authority; insubordinate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German upstutzig. Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk oppstuss. By surface analysis, upp + studsig.
From Old Swedish upstandilse, calque of Middle Low German upstannisse, equivalent to uppstå(nda) + -else
From Old Swedish upsāt, from Middle Low German upsat.

Compound of ur (“aurochs”) + oxe (“ox”), calque of Middle Low German ūrosse (compare English aurochs), with the first element being the original word for the species, from Late Old Swedish ur, uhr, presumed from an earlier Old Swedish *ūrer m (based on dialectal ure m), from Old Norse úrr, from Prot
From Old Swedish utgipt, from Middle Low German utgift, equivalent to ut + gift. Related to the verbs utge and ge ut.
From Middle Low German wachte, from Old Saxon wahta, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.
Borrowed from Middle Low German wachtele, from Old Saxon *hwahtula, from Proto-West Germanic *hwahtlā.

parole.significato: lifestyle, way of life (from a moral standpoint), (when sounding better as a translation) conduct
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German wandel. Cognate of German Wandel. Related to the verb vandla, now obsolete except for as the second part of förvandla and omvandla.
From Old Swedish vandra, borrowed from Middle Low German wanderen, from Old Saxon *wandarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn.

parole.significato: to stroll, to wander, to walk without hurry
parole.testo: From Old Swedish vanka, probably borrowed from Middle Low German wanken, from Old Saxon wankon, from Proto-West Germanic *wankōn, from Proto-Germanic *wankōną, cognate with Danish vanke and Old Norse vakka.
From Middle Low German wankelmot or German Wankelmut. Cognate of Dutch wankelmoed.
From Old Swedish vansinnogher, from Middle Low German wansinnich, equivalent to van- + -sinnig. Cognate with German wahnsinnig, Dutch waanzinnig.
Inherited from Old Swedish vara, from Middle Low German waren, from Old Saxon waron, from Proto-Germanic *warōną. Cognate with Danish vare.

parole.significato: a werewolf (human (at times) transformed into a wolf-like form)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German warwulf, from Old Saxon werwulf.
From Old Swedish vidhergiælda, a calque of Middle Low German weddergelden (“pay in return”), equivalent to veder- + gälla. Compare English payback.

parole.significato: to refresh, to invigorate, to quicken, to recreate (give new strength to)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish vidherqvekia, a calque of Middle Low German wedderquicken, equivalent to veder- + kvick + -a. Compare Danish vederkvæge.

From Middle Low German wedderwerdich. Cognate of German widerwärtig. First half of compound related to veder-, second half of compound cognate with German -wärtig, Gothic -𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸𐍃 (-wairþs), English -ward. Original meaning literally "turned against". Compare vidrig, English witherward, Gothic 𐍅𐌹𐌸𐍂𐌰𐍅𐌰
From Middle Low German wēmōt, whence also German Wehmut (which see). Analysable as ve (“woe”) + mod (“mood”). See also Old English wéamód (“angry, wrathful”).
From verk + stad, based on the Middle Low German werkstede. Compare English workstead and German Werkstatt.

parole.significato: knowledge (awareness of a particular fact or specific information about something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish vitskaper, from Middle Low German witschap, witschop, equivalent to vett + -skap. Cognate with Danish vidskap.
Previously also written vidlöftig, used since 1555. From Middle Low German wîtluftich, same as German weitläufig.
Inherited from Old Swedish vilkor, from Middle Low German willekōr, willekōre. Cognate of Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk vilkår, German Willkür.
Inherited from Old Swedish vilkora, from Middle Low German willekoren. By surface analysis, villkor + -a.
From Old Swedish vinka, from Middle Low German winken, from Proto-Germanic *winkōną.
From Middle Low German winkel, from Old Saxon *winkil, from Proto-West Germanic *winkil, from Proto-Indo-European *weng-.

parole.significato: to wind (yarn on a roll), to roll
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle Low German wīre, Middle Low German wīren, cognate to English wire.

parole.significato: surely, certainly, admittedly Signals a concession and in the following clause a counterpoint usually headed by men (“b…
parole.testo: Partly from Old Swedish visselika, partly from Middle Low German wisseliken. The -r- is due to the analogical influence of adverbs like innerligen (“innerly”) and veterligen (“as far as one knows”). By surface analysis, viss (“certain”) + -lig (adjectival suffix) + -en (adverbial suffix).
From Middle Low German wevel, wêvel, wivel, from Old Saxon *wivil.

parole.significato: guard, member of security (in charge of property)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish vaktare, væktare, from Middle Low German wechter or German Wächter, equivalent to vakta + -are. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål vekter and Norwegian Nynorsk vektar, see also Swedish vakt (“guard”).

parole.significato: huge; of a very large size
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German weldich, whence also Danish vældig and Norwegian Bokmål veldig (which are usually used in a different way from the Swedish word). See the related German gewaltig (“enormous”) for more.
Borrowed from Middle Low German wert (genitive: werdes), from Old Saxon werd or wird. Cognate with Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (wairdus), German Wirt, Dutch waard.

parole.significato: to recruit, to get to join
parole.testo: From Old Swedish værva, from Middle Low German werven and Middle High German werben, from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną. Doublet of värva, which is a homonym.

Inherited from Old Swedish väsende, väsent. Derived from Middle Low German wesen, wesent (“to be”); or German Wesen (“being; essence; character”) from Middle High German wesen (“to be, become”) from Old High German wesan (“to be, exists”). First attested in 1526.
From Middle Low German wesentlich, wesentlich. By surface analysis, väsen + lig.

parole.significato: a bag (for carrying belongings, etc., usually able to be opened and closed and with a handle or strap)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German veske.
From Middle Low German wōnunge, wāninge, from Old Saxon *wonunga, *wununga, from Proto-West Germanic *wunungu. Cognate with English woning, German Wohnung, Dutch woning.

parole.significato: genuine, authentic; not faked or counterfeit
parole.testo: From older spelling ekta, from Middle Low German echt, from Proto-West Germanic *aiwahaft. Cognate with Icelandic ekta, Norwegian Nynorsk ekte and Danish ægte.

From Old Swedish äktaskap, a calque of Middle Low German echteschap, equivalent to äkta (“married”) + -skap (“-hood”). Likely influenced by words like vetenskap, räkenskap, and dryckenskap. Compare Danish ægteskab, Norwegian ekteskap.

Inherited from Old Swedish ämbar, from Middle Low German [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *ambrī, likely borrowed from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μφορεύς (ămphoreús). Doublet of amfora. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ambar and Riksmål Norwegian amber.

From Middle Low German endeliken, from ende, near-equivalent to ändlig (“finite”) + -en (adverbial suffix). Cognate with Danish endelig, Norwegian Bokmål endelig, Norwegian Nynorsk endeleg, German endlich, Dutch eindelijk and English endly.

parole.significato: honor, glory; an objectification of praiseworthiness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German ēre, from Old Saxon ēra (“renown, glory, honor”). Cognate with Icelandic æra and Faroese æra.
From Old Swedish ærogirugher, from Middle Low German erengirich, equivalent to ära + -e- + girig. Cognate of Danish ærgerrig and German ehrgierig. See also German ehrgeizig.
Perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German *ervetlik, a form of Middle Low German *erventlik, from the Middle Low German ervent (“heir”). Compare Danish arvelig.
From Old Swedish ǣrlīker, from Middle Low German êrlich, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀulīk, equivalent to ära + -lig. Cognate of German ehrlich.

parole.significato: request (in particular a certain amount of money)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æskia (“to demand; to invite”), from Middle Low German eschen or Middle Low German eischen, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn. Cognate with English ask.
From Middle Low German even, effen, from Old Saxon evan, from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, cognate with English even, Dutch even. Compare Danish effen. See also jämn.

parole.significato: an old volume measure for fluids (157 litres)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German am, ame. Cf. Dutch aam.

parole.significato: a moment, an instant, a blink of an eye (very brief period of time)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German ōgenblik, equivalent to ögon + blick. Of same origin as Icelandic augnablik, Norwegian Nynorsk augneblikk and Danish øjeblik, whence Norwegian Bokmål øyeblikk. Compare also Dutch ogenblik, German Augenblick, Yiddish אויגנבליק (oygnblik), English eyeblink.

parole.significato: to practice, to train to do something, to exercise
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ȫven, from Old Saxon ōbian, from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną (“to do, practice”), see also German üben (“to practice”).
Used at least since 1722, borrowed from Middle Low German, compare with German überall, Danish overalt, Afrikaans oral and Dutch overal.
From Old Swedish ower ens, calque of Middle Low German over en, equivalent of över + ens.
Inherited from Old Swedish ivirflöþ, ivirflöþe, from Middle Low German övervlōt. Compare Latin superfluitas, German Überfluss. See also överflöda, överflödig.

parole.significato: overestimation of one's abilities (leading to unwise decisions), overconfidence
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ivirmodh, overmodh, from Middle Low German overmot, equivalent to över- + mod. Cognate with Danish overmod.
Inherited from Old Swedish ovir māto, from Middle Low German overmate, literally "beyond measure".

parole.significato: to translate; to change from one language to another, usually written text
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ȫversetten, ōversetten, from Old Saxon *ovarsettian, from Proto-West Germanic *ubarsattjan. Equivalent to över + sätta. Cognate with English overset, German übersetzen.
From Middle Low German overtügen. Compare German überzeugen, Dutch overtuigen.
From Middle Low German overweldigen, German überwältigen. Compare välde.
Calque of Middle Low German överich or German übrig, equivalent to över + -ig.

From Old Swedish bereþa, from Middle Low German bereden, from berede + -en or from be- + reden, equivalent to be- + reda. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål berede, Danish berede, Dutch bereiden, German bereiten.
Inherited from Old Swedish batsman, either from Middle Low German bōsman or Middle Dutch bōtsman. Equivalent to båt + -s- + man. Compare English boatsman, Dutch bootsman, German Bootsmann.

parole.significato: Inseparable verbal prefix that indicates an emphasizing meaning
parole.testo: From German er-, from Old High German ir-, and/or from Middle Low German er-, from Old Saxon ā-, both from Proto-Germanic *uz-.

From Old Swedish fīka f, fīkon n (plural), from Old Norse fíka, fíkja; formed using the fruit suffix + -on (neutral noun-forming suffix; used in the names of fruits and berries), an archaic variation from Old Norse -in. Originally either from Old English fīc or Vulgar Latin *fīca based on the -k- fo
From Middle Low German finne or from German Finne, perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *finnō. Related to English fin.
Either derived from Middle Low German vorbloden or German verbluten. Equivalent to för- + blöda. Cognate of Danish forbløde. See also English forbleed.
Superficially equivalent to för- + färdig + -a, from either Middle Low German vorverdigen or German verfertigen. Cognate of Danish forfærdige.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vorneme or from German vornehm. Cognate of Danish fornem. Originally with the sense "which can or should be taken before others".

parole.significato: a card; a piece of stiff paper or plastic.
parole.testo: Probably from Danish kort (“a card”) or possibly from a not referenced Middle Low German word kort known in Low German, kort (“a card”). Cognate with Icelandic kort (“a card, a map”) and Faroese kort (“a card, a map”), both from Old Norse kort (“a map”), all based on a variant of the Latin words cha

parole.significato: a manger, a crib, a feeding trough for animals
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krubba, from Old Norse krubba, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ. Cognate with German Krippe, English crib. Alternatively, perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German krübbe, kribbe, from Old Saxon kribbia, from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ.

From Old Swedish krønika, krønik, from Middle Low German kröneke ~ kroneke, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “relating to time”), derived from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Compare Danish and Norwegian krønike. It is not ruled out that the word was borrowed into Old Saxon ear

Borrowed from Low German rēling, regeling or from Dutch reeling, regeling, from Middle Low German regel, from Old Saxon *rigil, probably borrowed from Latin regula (“bar, rule”). Cognate of German Reling, English railing, Danish ræling.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smuk or from German Schmuck. Cognate of Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk smykke.

parole.significato: to flush (let water (or another liquid) flow over, usually in order clean, and usually at pressure), (when cleaning) to…
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German spölen, from Old Saxon spōlian, from Proto-West Germanic *spōlijan. Compare the older byform spöla. The back vowel could stem from Low German past forms with Rückumlaut. Alternatively it could be from Middle Dutch influence. Cognate with Danish spule, Norwegian Bokmål

parole.significato: to mutilate, to curtail, to shorten
parole.testo: Either borrowed from German stümpfen, related to German Stumpf (“stump”), or inherited from Old Swedish stympla, borrowed from Middle Low German stumpelen (from whence German verstümmeln).

parole.significato: stand; be in an upright position
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stā, possibly from an unattested eastern Old Norse stá, or via early Middle Low German stān. Both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stāną, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-. Or from earlier Swedish stånda, from Old Swedish staanda, standa, stonda, from Old Norse standa, from Proto-Germ
From either Middle Low German swans or German Schwanz.
From Low German tuten, from Middle Low German tūten, either of imitative origin or derived from Proto-West Germanic *þeutan (“to howl”), itself probably imitative.

parole.significato: to think (think to oneself, have a thought (process) in one's head)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þænkia, from Middle Low German denken (“to perceive, think”), from Old Saxon thenkian. While nk attests to the Low German origin, the initial t must be due to influence by some inherited cognate. This is probably either tycka (“to have an opinion”) or Old Swedish þækkia (“to seem, t
Likely from Middle Low German wankelmōdich or possibly from German wankelmütig.

Possibly of Middle Low German origin (cf. Middle Low German adel), from Old Saxon ethiling, from Proto-West Germanic *aþuling, from Proto-Germanic *aþulingaz; alternatively from Old Norse ǫðlingr, ultimately from the same Proto-Germanic root.
